stem: A media company serves a CloudFront distribution with an S3 origin for video segments and a second cache behavior for /api/* that forwards to an ALB origin returning personalized data. The API response varies only by a sessionId query string parameter, but many other tracking query strings are appended by the client. The team wants to maximize the cache hit ratio for the /api/* behavior while still personalizing correctly. What should they configure?

choices.text: A cache policy for /api/* that forwards all query strings to the origin
An origin request policy forwarding User-Agent and Referer instead of query strings
Disable caching for /api/* and forward every request to the origin
A cache policy for /api/* whose cache key includes only the sessionId query string

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A cache policy for /api/* whose cache key includes only the session-relevant value keeps responses correctly separated while maximizing cache hits.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Forward all query strings in the cache key: fragments the cache.
• Origin request policy only: doesn't change the cache key.
• Disable caching: loses all offload.

Key takeaway: keep cache keys minimal but correct.

stem: A gaming company is building a real-time multiplayer title that uses a custom UDP protocol on a fixed set of ports. Clients need a small set of static anycast IP addresses to hardcode into the game client, and traffic must fail over to healthy endpoints in another Region within seconds if a Region becomes impaired. There is no HTTP traffic and no need for content caching. Which edge networking service best fits this requirement?

choices.text: Application Load Balancer with cross-zone load balancing
AWS Global Accelerator
Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing
Amazon CloudFront with a custom origin

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs and routes custom UDP traffic over the AWS backbone to the nearest healthy endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ALB: HTTP only.
• Route 53 latency: DNS only, no acceleration.
• CloudFront: HTTP(S).

Key takeaway: global UDP → Global Accelerator.

stem: A public app runs on an ALB in eu-central-1 without CloudFront. Security must block SQL injection and rate-limit IPs, and the web ACL must be managed centrally by Firewall Manager. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: Shield Advanced alone, which includes SQLi managed rules
A CLOUDFRONT-scoped web ACL in us-east-1 associated with the ALB
A web ACL associated with the VPC route table
A REGIONAL web ACL in eu-central-1 on the ALB, via Firewall Manager

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ALBs use REGIONAL web ACLs in their own Region. Firewall Manager policies can deploy and enforce WAF web ACLs on in-scope ALBs across accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CLOUDFRONT scope: only for CloudFront distributions.
• Route tables: WAF associates with resources, not route tables.
• Shield Advanced alone: DDoS protection, not SQLi rules.

Key takeaway: ALB WAF = REGIONAL in its Region.

stem: A CloudFront distribution is configured with an origin group containing a primary S3 origin and a secondary S3 origin in another Region for disaster recovery. During a test, the primary bucket is made to return HTTP 403 responses for all objects, but CloudFront continues serving the 403 errors to viewers instead of failing over to the secondary origin. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: CloudFront origin groups only fail over based on TCP connection timeouts, never HTTP status codes
The origin group's failover criteria does not include the 403 status code
Origin groups only support ALB and EC2 custom origins, not S3 origins
The secondary origin's bucket policy blocks CloudFront's OAC

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Origin groups fail over only on the status codes listed in the failover criteria. If 403 isn't included, CloudFront won't fail over on it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• TCP-only failover: status codes are supported.
• No S3 origins: S3 is supported.
• OAC blocked on secondary: would fail after failover, not prevent it.

Key takeaway: include the right status codes in failover criteria.

stem: An engineering team needs to call an external third-party fraud-detection API and inspect the response body before forwarding a request to their origin, adding significant per-request latency and requiring outbound network calls from the edge. Which CloudFront edge compute feature should they use, and why can the alternative not be used?

choices.text: CloudFront Functions, which support outbound calls to third-party APIs
CloudFront Functions on origin-response, with more memory and time than Lambda@Edge
Lambda@Edge on origin-request; CloudFront Functions can't make network calls
Lambda@Edge on viewer-response only, since origin-request isn't supported

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront Functions can't make network calls. Lambda@Edge on origin-request can call the external API and act on its response.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Functions with outbound calls: not supported.
• Functions on origin-response: Functions run only on viewer events.
• Origin-request unsupported: it's supported for Lambda@Edge.

Key takeaway: network calls at the edge → Lambda@Edge.

stem: A game studio wants to expose thousands of backend game server instances behind a small set of static IP addresses, preserve the original client IP address end to end, and map incoming client connections directly to specific instance IP:port combinations without deploying a load balancer in front of the fleet. Which Global Accelerator feature satisfies this?

choices.text: A standard accelerator with client affinity set to SOURCE_IP
A custom routing accelerator that maps listener port ranges to specific instance IPs and ports
A standard accelerator with Elastic IP endpoints and health checks disabled
A standard accelerator with a Network Load Balancer endpoint

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A custom routing accelerator maps listener port ranges to specific EC2 destinations, letting clients reach individual game servers behind a few static IPs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SOURCE_IP affinity: doesn't target specific servers.
• EIP endpoints: standard accelerators balance, not map.
• NLB endpoint: balances across targets.

Key takeaway: deterministic mapping to specific instances → custom routing accelerator.

stem: A CloudFront distribution has cache behaviors configured in this order: a default behavior (*) that caches based on all headers with a short TTL, followed by a behavior for the path pattern /images/*. Static images under /images/ are being served with the default behavior's short TTL and low cache hit ratio instead of the long-TTL image-optimized behavior. What is the root cause and fix?

choices.text: CloudFront orders behaviors by specificity automatically
Every pattern needs a trailing wildcard, so /images/* is invalid and falls to default
Behaviors are evaluated in listed order; move /images/* above the default
The /images/* behavior needs an explicit precedence value in a separate field

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront evaluates cache behaviors in the listed precedence order. Move /images/* above broader patterns so it matches first.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Automatic specificity ordering: not applied.
• Trailing wildcard invalid: it's valid.
• Separate precedence field in another setting: order is the precedence.

Key takeaway: behavior order = precedence.

stem: A CloudFront distribution serves only North American and European customers. The company wants to cut costs without blocking anyone. Which setting fits, and what is the trade-off?

choices.text: A Price Class that excludes other regions; distant viewers get higher latency
A shorter TTL to reduce edge usage
Geo restriction allowing only North America and Europe, blocking all other viewers
Origin Shield in South America

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Price classes limit which edge locations serve content, lowering cost. Viewers elsewhere are still served, from the nearest included edge, with higher latency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Geo restriction: blocks users, which isn't wanted.
• Shorter TTL: increases origin fetches and cost.
• Origin Shield: adds a caching layer, not an edge limit.

Key takeaway: cheaper edges without blocking → Price Class.

stem: A CloudFront distribution's origin is an on-premises data center reached over Direct Connect. During peak hours, the origin experiences high request volume even though CloudFront edge caches show a reasonable overall hit ratio, because many different edge locations around the world each experience their first cache miss for the same rarely-changing objects and hit the origin independently. Which feature should be enabled to reduce this origin load?

choices.text: A second CloudFront distribution pointed at the same origin to split traffic
Signed URLs with a short expiration
Origin Shield, placed in a Region close to the origin
Field-level encryption on the cache behavior

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Origin Shield adds a central caching layer near the origin, collapsing requests from edge locations and reducing load on the on-premises origin.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Second distribution: doubles origin load.
• Signed URLs: access control.
• Field-level encryption: data protection.

Key takeaway: protect a constrained origin → Origin Shield.

stem: A team wants to send 5% of production traffic to a new backend, then 25%, then 100%, with the ability to roll back instantly, using DNS. Which Route 53 setup fits, and what limits rollback speed?

choices.text: Failover records with the new version as secondary, promoted by health checks
Latency records per version
Geolocation records by continent
Weighted records with health checks; DNS TTL caching slows shifts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Weighted routing splits DNS answers by weight, so changing weights shifts traffic. Resolver caching of the TTL delays how fast changes take effect, so use low TTLs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Latency: routes by performance, not by percentage.
• Failover: all-or-nothing.
• Geolocation: splits by location, not percentage.

Key takeaway: percentage shifts in DNS → weighted records; keep TTLs low.

stem: A company has application stacks deployed in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. They currently use geolocation routing but want to be able to gradually shift a small, controlled percentage of traffic from one Region to the other for a capacity test, without changing which physical Region actually serves which countries. Which Route 53 capability should they use instead?

choices.text: Latency-based routing with health checks disabled
Geoproximity routing with a bias value, configured through a Traffic Flow policy
Geolocation routing with fewer country-level records
Simple routing with two A records for the same name

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Geoproximity routing with a bias expands or shrinks the area routed to each Region, shifting traffic gradually (configured via Traffic Flow).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Latency without health checks: no control over shift.
• Fewer geolocation records: coarse.
• Simple routing: no control.

Key takeaway: shift geographic boundaries → geoproximity bias.

stem: A company is migrating workloads to a VPC and wants on-premises servers to resolve records hosted in a Route 53 private hosted zone associated with that VPC, without exposing the zone publicly. What should they configure?

choices.text: A public hosted zone with the same name and NS delegation from on-premises DNS
A Resolver inbound endpoint plus on-prem conditional forwarding to it
AWS Site-to-Site VPN with DNS64 enabled on the connection
A Resolver outbound endpoint with a forwarding rule to on-premises DNS servers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Resolver inbound endpoint receives queries forwarded from on-premises DNS (via conditional forwarders) and resolves the private hosted zone.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public zone: exposes records.
• DNS64 on VPN: unrelated.
• Outbound endpoint: for VPC to on-premises.

Key takeaway: on-prem → AWS private zones = inbound endpoint.

stem: A company registered its domain with a third-party registrar and hosts its zone in Route 53. They have enabled DNSSEC signing on the hosted zone, which created a customer-managed KSK backed by AWS KMS and Route 53-managed ZSKs. Which additional step is required for validating resolvers to establish the full chain of trust?

choices.text: Nothing; enabling DNSSEC signing in Route 53 completes the chain of trust
Rotate the ZSK manually before the chain of trust can be established
Create a CNAME record pointing to the KMS key ARN
Add Route 53's DS record at the third-party registrar

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Completing the DNSSEC chain of trust requires adding Route 53's DS record at the parent zone through the registrar.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Nothing more: the parent must have the DS record.
• Rotate the ZSK: unrelated.
• CNAME to a KMS ARN: meaningless.

Key takeaway: DNSSEC needs the DS record in the parent.

stem: A security team wants resources inside a VPC to be blocked from resolving known malicious domains, while allowing an explicit allow-list of approved external domains for API integrations, all enforced at the DNS layer before a connection is even attempted. Which service should they configure?

choices.text: Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall domain lists on the VPC
VPC Flow Logs with a Lambda function that terminates matching connections
Security groups with FQDN-based outbound rules
AWS Network Firewall with stateful domain filtering rules only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall blocks queries to domains in block lists for VPCs while allowing others.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flow Logs with Lambda: reactive.
• SG FQDN rules: not supported.
• Network Firewall only: works for traffic, but DNS Firewall directly blocks resolution.

Key takeaway: block malicious domain resolution → DNS Firewall.

stem: A Route 53 failover routing configuration has a primary record with an associated health check and a secondary record. During an incident, the primary endpoint is actually healthy and reachable from the internet, but Route 53 still marks the health check as unhealthy and fails traffic over to the secondary. What is a likely cause to investigate first?

choices.text: The secondary record's TTL is set too low for failover to occur
The zone is private, and private zones don't support failover routing at all
Failover routing doesn't support health checks on the primary record
The primary's security group blocks Route 53 health checker IPs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Route 53 health checkers must reach the endpoint. If the security group blocks their IP ranges, the check fails or behaves unexpectedly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Low secondary TTL: speeds failover.
• Private zones don't support failover: they do (with CloudWatch-alarm checks).
• No health checks on primary: required.

Key takeaway: allow Route 53 health checker IPs.

stem: A shared services account owns a Route 53 Resolver rule that conditionally forwards queries for corp.example.com to on-premises DNS servers via an outbound endpoint. The rule has been shared with several spoke accounts using AWS RAM. Instances in one spoke VPC still fail to resolve corp.example.com, while instances in another spoke VPC that received the same shared rule resolve it correctly. What configuration step was most likely missed for the failing VPC?

choices.text: The outbound endpoint needs a separate IP address allocated per consuming VPC
The Resolver rule must be associated with the failing VPC in addition to being shared via RAM
RAM sharing does not support Resolver rules, so a duplicate rule must be created in the spoke account
Security groups on the Resolver outbound endpoint must allow traffic from the spoke VPC's CIDR

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A shared Resolver rule must also be associated with each VPC that should use it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IP per VPC: not required.
• RAM doesn't share rules: it does.
• Endpoint SGs: would affect all VPCs.

Key takeaway: share and then associate Resolver rules.

stem: A team needs DNS load balancing across 8 web server IPs, with unhealthy IPs removed automatically, and clients receiving several IPs per answer. No load balancer is allowed. Which routing fits?

choices.text: Simple routing with one record holding 8 IPs
Multivalue answer with a health check per record
Weighted routing with equal weights and a health check on each record
Latency routing across the 8 records

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Multivalue answer returns up to 8 healthy records per query and omits records whose health checks fail, providing basic DNS-level load distribution.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Simple routing: returns all values with no health checking.
• Weighted: returns one record per query.
• Latency: routes by Region, not across 8 servers.

Key takeaway: multiple healthy IPs per answer → multivalue.

stem: Account A owns a Route 53 private hosted zone that needs to be resolvable from a VPC that lives in Account B. What two actions, in order, are required to associate Account B's VPC with Account A's private hosted zone? (Select TWO)

choices.text: In Account B, call the API to associate the VPC with the hosted zone, referencing the hosted zone ID from Account A
In Account A, delete and recreate the hosted zone as a shared resource
In Account B, share the VPC with Account A using AWS RAM before any authorization can be created
In Account A, create a VPC association authorization for Account B's VPC and the hosted zone
In Account A, manually add Account B's VPC CIDR as an allowed network ACL entry on the hosted zone

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account PHZ association: Account A creates a VPC association authorization for B's VPC, and Account B associates the VPC with the zone.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Recreate zone as shared: not needed.
• Share VPC with RAM: not needed.
• Add CIDR: not how PHZ works.

Key takeaway: cross-account PHZ = authorize (owner) + associate (VPC owner).

stem: A global application uses Route 53 latency-based routing with records in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. After deploying a new stack in ap-southeast-1, users in Australia continue to be routed to the us-east-1 endpoint even though the new ap-southeast-1 endpoint would provide much lower latency for them. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: Latency routing always prefers the first record created, regardless of latency
Latency routing requires at least three records before it activates
Australian resolvers cache answers until a DNS Firewall rule clears them
There's no latency record for the ap-southeast-1 endpoint

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Latency routing chooses among existing records. Without an ap-southeast-1 record, Australian users get the lowest-latency existing Region.

Why the other options are wrong:
• First record preferred: false.
• Three records needed: false.
• DNS Firewall caching: unrelated.

Key takeaway: add a latency record for each endpoint Region.

stem: An application requires the true client source IP address to be visible at the TCP layer without parsing HTTP headers, needs to preserve extremely low latency, and must pass through TLS untouched end to end to the backend. Which load balancer type should be used, and why is the alternative unsuitable?

choices.text: NLB, which preserves the client source IP natively at Layer 4
NLB, because it terminates TLS and re-encrypts to targets with ACM
ALB, which adds an X-Forwarded-For header with the client IP
ALB with proxy protocol v2, which ALB supports natively

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An NLB preserves the client source IP at Layer 4 for most target types, so the application sees it without parsing headers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NLB re-encrypting with ACM: not the reason.
• ALB X-Forwarded-For: requires header parsing.
• ALB proxy protocol v2: ALB doesn't send it.

Key takeaway: client IP at L4 → NLB.

stem: A security team wants to insert third-party virtual firewall appliances transparently in front of multiple VPCs to inspect all traffic, with the appliance fleet scaling automatically based on load, using GENEVE encapsulation to preserve the original packet for inspection. Which load balancing service is purpose-built for this?

choices.text: Application Load Balancer with a Lambda target
Classic Load Balancer with an auto scaling group of appliances
Gateway Load Balancer
Network Load Balancer with UDP listeners

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gateway Load Balancer transparently inserts and scales third-party appliances in the traffic path.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ALB with Lambda: not appliances.
• CLB with ASG: not transparent.
• NLB UDP: not transparent insertion.

Key takeaway: inline appliances → GWLB.

stem: A team is deciding whether to enable cross-zone load balancing on a Network Load Balancer that currently has an uneven number of registered targets per Availability Zone, causing some targets to receive disproportionately more traffic. What is the tradeoff of enabling cross-zone load balancing on this NLB?

choices.text: NLB cross-zone load balancing cannot be changed after creation
Enabling it disables preservation of the client source IP address
It is free and affects only health check frequency, not traffic distribution
More even distribution, but cross-AZ traffic incurs data transfer charges

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-zone load balancing distributes traffic evenly across all targets, but NLB cross-AZ traffic incurs data transfer charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't change: configurable.
• Disables client IP preservation: no.
• Free and only health checks: incorrect.

Key takeaway: NLB cross-zone = even load vs. cross-AZ cost.

stem: An application team changed a target group's health check path from /status to /health as part of a routine cleanup, but the application only implements a health endpoint at /status. Shortly after, all targets in the target group are marked unhealthy and the ALB begins returning 503 errors to clients. What is the correct fix?

choices.text: Increase the healthy threshold count so targets are marked healthy faster
Restore the /status path, or implement a working /health endpoint
Leave the path and check the deregistration delay setting instead
Increase the health check timeout to 300 seconds

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If /health doesn't exist, all targets fail health checks. Restore /status or implement a working /health endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Healthy threshold: doesn't fix a 404.
• Deregistration delay: unrelated.
• 300-second timeout: invalid and irrelevant.

Key takeaway: health check path must exist.

stem: A shopping app behind an ALB must keep users on the same target for 30 minutes. The app already issues its own session cookie named SESSIONID. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: Duration-based stickiness, since ALB can't use app cookies
Source-IP stickiness on the target group
Stickiness is only available on NLB
Application-based stickiness using the SESSIONID cookie

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ALB supports application-based cookie stickiness, where it follows a cookie your application sets (and uses AWSALBAPP), as well as duration-based stickiness with its own AWSALB cookie.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Duration-based only: ALB also supports application cookies.
• Source-IP: NLB feature, not ALB.
• NLB only: ALB supports stickiness.

Key takeaway: reuse the app's cookie → application-based stickiness.

stem: During a rolling deployment behind an ALB, instances are deregistered from the target group as new instances come online. Users report dropped connections and failed in-flight requests at the moment old instances are deregistered, even though the deployment tooling waits for new targets to become healthy first. What setting should be adjusted to fix this?

choices.text: Enable cross-zone load balancing on the target group
Decrease the health check interval on the target group
Increase the deregistration delay (connection draining)
Switch from an Application Load Balancer to an NLB

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A longer deregistration delay lets in-flight requests finish before targets are removed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cross-zone: unrelated.
• Shorter interval: unrelated.
• Switch to NLB: same issue.

Key takeaway: graceful removal → deregistration delay.

stem: A partner must allow-list a small fixed set of IPs for your internet-facing endpoint, and you also need TLS termination with ACM and path routing. Which design fits?

choices.text: An ALB with Elastic IPs assigned per AZ
NLB with Elastic IPs in front of an ALB target
A Gateway Load Balancer with static IPs
A Classic Load Balancer with fixed IPs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
NLBs support one static or Elastic IP per AZ. An ALB can be registered as an NLB target, combining fixed IPs with ALB features such as path routing (TLS can terminate on the ALB with ACM).

Why the other options are wrong:
• ALB with EIPs: ALBs don't support Elastic IPs.
• GWLB: for appliances.
• CLB: no static IPs.

Key takeaway: static IPs + L7 features → NLB in front of ALB (or Global Accelerator).

stem: One ALB serves api.example.com and www.example.com. The certificate must cover both names, and routing must split by name. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: Path rules on /api and /www prefixes
Query-string rules to identify the site
Host-header rules plus SNI with a certificate per name
Two ALBs, one per domain name, sharing one wildcard certificate

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Host-based rules route by the Host header, and ALB HTTPS listeners support multiple certificates with SNI, or one certificate covering both names.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Path rules: the names differ, not the paths.
• Two ALBs: unnecessary cost.
• Query strings: not how clients distinguish sites.

Key takeaway: name-based routing → host-header rules + SNI.

stem: A centralized inspection architecture routes VPC traffic through Gateway Load Balancer endpoints to a fleet of stateful firewall appliances behind a Gateway Load Balancer. Engineers observe that some flows are inspected correctly, but for other flows the return traffic takes a different path through a different Availability Zone than the outbound leg, causing the stateful firewall to drop the traffic as unrecognized. What should be enabled to fix this?

choices.text: Source-IP stickiness on the GWLB target group
Cross-zone load balancing on the Gateway Load Balancer
A dedicated NAT gateway per AZ in the inspection VPC
Appliance mode, keeping each flow on the same target and AZ

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Appliance mode on the TGW attachment keeps both directions of a flow on the same AZ, so the same stateful appliance sees the whole flow.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Source-IP stickiness: GWLB already hashes flows; asymmetry comes from TGW.
• Cross-zone on GWLB: doesn't fix TGW asymmetry.
• NAT per AZ: unrelated.

Key takeaway: stateful inspection via TGW → appliance mode.

stem: A team is choosing between terminating TLS at an Application Load Balancer versus passing TLS through end to end on a Network Load Balancer. Terminating at the ALB allows centralized certificate management with ACM and enables host- and path-based routing, but the team is concerned about compliance requirements for true end-to-end encryption. What is the correct tradeoff assessment?

choices.text: NLB cannot handle TLS at all, so ALB termination is the only option
NLB passthrough keeps end-to-end TLS but loses L7; ALB gives L7 and central certs
ALB termination always keeps end-to-end encryption, since ACM is used on both legs
No difference; both always re-encrypt to backends with ACM certificates

explanation:
Why this is correct:
NLB TLS passthrough keeps encryption end to end but gives up Layer 7 features. ALB termination enables L7 routing and WAF, with re-encryption to targets optional.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NLB can't handle TLS: it can.
• ALB always end-to-end: it terminates.
• No difference: they differ.

Key takeaway: passthrough vs. L7 features.

stem: A security team needs VPC Flow Logs delivered to a third-party SIEM in near real time via a streaming pipeline, while a separate compliance team needs the same flow log data retained cheaply for seven years and queried occasionally with Amazon Athena. Which two flow log destinations should be configured to meet both needs? (Select TWO)

choices.text: CloudWatch Logs only, used for both streaming and retention
Data Firehose streaming to the SIEM
AWS Config, for long-term retention and Athena querying
Amazon S3 with Athena for retention
AWS CloudTrail, for both real-time streaming and long-term retention

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data Firehose streams flow logs to the SIEM in near real time, and S3 with Athena provides low-cost long-term retention and querying.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudWatch Logs for both: costly retention and not a streaming pipeline to the SIEM.
• Config: configuration, not flow logs.
• CloudTrail: API calls.

Key takeaway: stream to SIEM + archive in S3.

stem: A company operates dozens of VPCs across multiple accounts and wants centralized, queryable logs of every DNS query made by resources within those VPCs, including the query name, response, and the instance that issued it, for security investigations. Which capability should they configure?

choices.text: AWS CloudTrail data events for Route 53
Resolver query logging to a central destination
VPC Flow Logs with the additional DNS fields enabled
Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall alert logs only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Resolver query logging records DNS queries from VPCs and can send them to a central destination (S3, CloudWatch Logs, Firehose), shared across accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail data events: not DNS queries.
• Flow log DNS fields: not available.
• DNS Firewall alerts only: only matched queries.

Key takeaway: all DNS queries → Resolver query logging.

stem: A global enterprise has dozens of Transit Gateways, Direct Connect connections, and Site-to-Site VPN connections spread across multiple Regions and accounts, along with on-premises SD-WAN devices. Leadership wants a single visual representation of the entire network topology and its real-time operational status. Which service should be used to build this?

choices.text: Reachability Analyzer run against each Transit Gateway individually
CloudWatch dashboards built manually for each Region
An AWS Config aggregator with a custom conformance pack
AWS Network Manager with a global network registering TGWs, sites, and links

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Network Manager's global network registers TGWs, sites, and connections, giving a global topology view with monitoring.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reachability Analyzer per TGW: not global.
• Manual dashboards: toil.
• Config aggregator: configuration.

Key takeaway: global network visibility → Network Manager.

stem: A network team wants to continuously measure packet loss and latency on the path between their AWS VPCs and an on-premises data center reached over Direct Connect, without deploying any monitoring agent or software on the on-premises servers themselves. Which capability fits this requirement?

choices.text: Direct Connect connection-level CloudWatch metrics only
VPC Flow Logs analyzed with Amazon Athena
AWS Network Manager Route Analyzer
CloudWatch Network Monitor probes deployed in the VPC

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudWatch Network Monitor probes measure packet loss and latency continuously between AWS and on-premises destinations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DX metrics only: link-level.
• Flow Logs with Athena: no latency or loss.
• Route Analyzer: route analysis.

Key takeaway: hybrid path latency/loss → Network Monitor.

stem: Security wants flow logs for every ENI in a VPC, including ENIs created later by Lambda and load balancers, with custom fields including pkt-srcaddr. What should be configured?

choices.text: Subnet-level flow logs for existing subnets only
One VPC-level flow log with a custom format
CloudTrail data events for EC2
Per-ENI flow logs added by an EventBridge rule

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A VPC-level flow log covers all current and future ENIs in the VPC, and custom formats can include fields such as pkt-srcaddr.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Per-ENI automation: fragile and unnecessary.
• Existing subnets only: misses new subnets.
• CloudTrail: logs API calls, not traffic.

Key takeaway: broadest coverage → VPC-level flow logs.

stem: Traffic between two VPC attachments on a Transit Gateway is intermittently failing, and the network team suspects packets are being dropped at the Transit Gateway itself rather than within either VPC. Which logging capability should be enabled to directly observe accepted and rejected traffic at the Transit Gateway level?

choices.text: AWS CloudTrail management events for the Transit Gateway
VPC Flow Logs on both VPCs, which capture TGW traffic natively
Transit Gateway Flow Logs, capturing traffic the TGW itself accepts or rejects
Route 53 Resolver query logging on the TGW attachments

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transit Gateway Flow Logs capture traffic the TGW itself processes, including drops, to diagnose attachment-to-attachment issues.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail: API calls.
• VPC Flow Logs capture TGW natively: not TGW decisions.
• Resolver logs: DNS.

Key takeaway: TGW traffic visibility → TGW Flow Logs.

stem: A network engineer suspects that traffic is not reaching its intended destination because of a missing or blackholed route somewhere along a multi-hop path through a Transit Gateway with several route tables. Rather than manually inspecting every route table, which tool can trace the expected path and identify the specific configuration issue?

choices.text: AWS Trusted Advisor network reachability checks
CloudWatch Logs Insights queries against VPC Flow Logs
VPC Reachability Analyzer only
AWS Network Manager Route Analyzer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Network Manager Route Analyzer analyzes TGW routes to show whether a path exists or where a route is missing or blackholed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: no.
• Logs Insights on flow logs: traffic, not routes.
• Reachability Analyzer only: VPC-focused paths; Route Analyzer targets TGW routes.

Key takeaway: TGW route problems → Route Analyzer.

stem: A platform team wants to proactively detect when traffic through a specific Transit Gateway VPC attachment is approaching its per-attachment bandwidth limit before applications experience throttling or packet loss. Which CloudWatch metrics should they monitor and alarm on?

choices.text: S3 request metrics for the flow log destination bucket
Per-attachment BytesIn/BytesOut/PacketDropCount
CPUUtilization of the EC2 instances behind the attachment
Route 53 health check status for the attachment

explanation:
Why this is correct:
TGW publishes per-attachment metrics such as BytesIn, BytesOut, and PacketDropCount, which CloudWatch alarms can monitor.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 request metrics: unrelated.
• EC2 CPU: unrelated.
• Route 53 health checks: unrelated.

Key takeaway: attachment health → TGW CloudWatch metrics.

stem: A large AWS Organization wants VPC Flow Logs from over 100 member accounts consolidated into a single central security account for analysis, without requiring each account team to manually configure cross-account permissions individually. What is an efficient way to achieve this centrally?

choices.text: Flow logs can't be delivered cross-account, so each account keeps its own
Deliver to a central S3 bucket whose policy allows the organization
Copy each account's flow logs manually every week using the AWS CLI
Have each account create a trust to the security account and email the ARNs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Flow logs can be delivered directly to a central S3 bucket whose policy allows delivery from all organization accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't deliver cross-account: they can.
• Manual weekly copies: toil.
• Email: no.

Key takeaway: central flow logs → org-wide bucket policy.

stem: A company wants to bundle two 10 Gbps dedicated connections into one 20 Gbps logical link and keep it up if one fails. Which option fits, and what are the constraints?

choices.text: A Transit Gateway Connect attachment
Two private VIFs advertising the same prefixes with equal BGP weights for ECMP
A Direct Connect gateway joining the two connections
A LAG: same speed, same DX endpoint; set minimum links

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A link aggregation group (LAG) combines dedicated connections of the same bandwidth terminating on the same AWS device into one logical interface. The minimum-links setting controls when the LAG stays operational.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DX gateway: connects to VPCs and TGWs; doesn't aggregate links.
• TGW Connect: GRE tunnels for SD-WAN.
• Two VIFs with ECMP-like weights: not a single logical link, and failure behavior differs.

Key takeaway: bundle physical links → LAG (same speed, same device).

stem: A company has a single Direct Connect connection and needs it to provide connectivity to VPCs located in five different AWS Regions across two accounts, using a single BGP session rather than one private VIF per VPC. Which Direct Connect construct is required?

choices.text: A Direct Connect gateway with a transit VIF, associated with each Region's TGW
Five private VIFs, one per Region, sharing the same BGP session
A hosted VIF for each additional Region beyond the first
Direct Connect SiteLink connecting each Region's VPC directly

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Direct Connect gateway with a transit VIF, associated with each Region's Transit Gateway, extends one connection to VPCs in multiple Regions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Five private VIFs sharing a BGP session: not how VIFs work.
• Hosted VIF per Region: unnecessary.
• SiteLink: site-to-site over the backbone.

Key takeaway: one DX, many Regions → DX gateway.

stem: An on-premises network advertises the same prefix to AWS over two Direct Connect private VIFs terminating at different AWS Direct Connect locations. The network team wants AWS to prefer sending return traffic over Connection A whenever it is available, only using Connection B if A is down. Which BGP technique achieves this preference for AWS-to-on-premises traffic?

choices.text: Increase the BGP keepalive interval on Connection B
Set a higher MED value on Connection A's advertisement
Configure a static route on the AWS side pointing only to Connection A
Prepend the on-premises ASN on routes advertised over Connection B

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AS path prepending on routes advertised over Connection B makes that path less preferred for traffic from AWS, so Connection A carries it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Keepalive interval: failure detection.
• Higher MED on A: makes A less preferred.
• Static route on AWS side: not configurable this way.

Key takeaway: influence AWS→on-prem path → AS path prepend.

stem: A company relies on a single Direct Connect connection for production traffic and wants a Site-to-Site VPN as an automatic backup path that only carries traffic when Direct Connect is unavailable, using dynamic BGP routing on both paths to the same VPC. How should this be configured so Direct Connect is preferred whenever healthy?

choices.text: BGP on both paths, with AS-path prepending on the VPN routes
Disable the VPN and enable it manually only during a Direct Connect outage
Use static routes on the VPN
Give the VPN the same BGP ASN as Direct Connect so AWS treats them as one path

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Running BGP on both paths and prepending the AS path on VPN advertisements makes DX preferred with automatic failover to VPN.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual VPN enabling: slow.
• Static VPN routes: may be preferred unexpectedly.
• Same ASN: not a preference mechanism.

Key takeaway: DX primary + VPN backup = BGP with prepending on VPN.

stem: A multinational company has Direct Connect connections established at Direct Connect locations in two different countries and wants to send traffic directly between those two on-premises sites through the AWS Direct Connect network backbone, without that traffic being routed through a VPC or an AWS Region. Which Direct Connect feature enables this?

choices.text: A Direct Connect Gateway with a private VIF in each Region
AWS Global Accelerator with custom routing
AWS Direct Connect SiteLink
Transit Gateway inter-Region peering

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Direct Connect SiteLink connects on-premises sites through DX locations over the AWS global network without going through a Region.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DX gateway with private VIFs: connects to VPCs, not site-to-site.
• Global Accelerator custom routing: not site-to-site.
• TGW peering: VPC traffic.

Key takeaway: site-to-site via DX locations → SiteLink.

stem: A regulated customer requires Layer 2 encryption on their Direct Connect connections to protect data in transit at line rate without the overhead of IPsec. Which Direct Connect feature should they enable, and what connection type is it supported on?

choices.text: TLS 1.3 termination at the Direct Connect router
MACsec on dedicated connections (e.g., 10/100 Gbps)
IPsec over Direct Connect on all hosted connections
MACsec, supported only on partner hosted connections

explanation:
Why this is correct:
MACsec provides Layer 2 encryption on supported dedicated connections (such as 10 and 100 Gbps).

Why the other options are wrong:
• TLS at the router: not L2.
• IPsec on hosted connections: L3, not L2.
• MACsec only on hosted connections: it's for dedicated connections.

Key takeaway: L2 encryption on DX → MACsec.

stem: A company uses SD-WAN appliances on-premises and wants to integrate them with a Transit Gateway using dynamic BGP routing over a GRE-based tunnel that supports higher throughput per tunnel than a standard Site-to-Site VPN attachment. Which Transit Gateway feature should they use?

choices.text: A Direct Connect transit VIF
Transit Gateway Connect (GRE with BGP)
A standard Site-to-Site VPN attachment with two tunnels for more bandwidth
A VPC peering connection between the SD-WAN VPC and the TGW VPC

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transit Gateway Connect attachments use GRE with BGP for high-throughput integration with SD-WAN appliances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transit VIF: DX, not SD-WAN overlay.
• Standard VPN: lower throughput.
• Peering: not a TGW attachment for SD-WAN.

Key takeaway: SD-WAN to TGW → Connect attachments.

stem: A hybrid network experiences intermittent BGP session flaps between an on-premises router and AWS over a Direct Connect connection, and each flap causes a 60-90 second outage while BGP hold timers expire before failover to a backup path completes. What should be implemented to detect the failure and trigger failover much faster?

choices.text: Switch from BGP to static routing to eliminate hold timers entirely
Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) alongside BGP on the VIF
Enable ECMP across the Direct Connect connection
Increase the BGP hold timer to 180 seconds to reduce false flaps

explanation:
Why this is correct:
BFD detects link failures in under a second, working alongside BGP for fast failover.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Static routing: loses dynamic failover.
• ECMP: load sharing.
• Longer hold timer: slower detection.

Key takeaway: fast failure detection → BFD.

stem: A company needs Direct Connect quickly, doesn't want to manage a cross-connect or port, and needs only 500 Mbps. Which option fits, and what does it give up?

choices.text: A partner hosted connection; no LAG or MACsec
A Site-to-Site VPN over a public VIF
A hosted VIF shared from another company's port
A dedicated 1 Gbps connection, which offers the same features

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Partner hosted connections come in speeds such as 500 Mbps, with the partner handling physical connectivity. LAGs and MACsec require dedicated connections.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Dedicated 1 Gbps: involves a cross-connect and port management.
• Hosted VIF: a virtual interface on someone else's connection, with shared capacity.
• VPN over a public VIF: still needs a DX connection.

Key takeaway: sub-1 Gbps, fast, managed → hosted connection.

stem: A company relies on Direct Connect with jumbo frames (9001 MTU) enabled end to end for a data replication workload that depends on high throughput. As a resiliency improvement, they add a Site-to-Site VPN as a BGP-advertised backup path to the same Transit Gateway. During a scheduled Direct Connect maintenance window, traffic fails over to the VPN and replication throughput drops sharply with intermittent errors related to oversized packets. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: The VPN must be re-established manually after each DX maintenance, so no traffic flowed
BGP can't fail over between DX and VPN
VPN tunnels don't support jumbo frames, so large packets fail
TGW VPN attachments don't support BGP, forcing static routing that drops large packets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
VPN tunnels don't support jumbo frames. When traffic fails over from DX to VPN, 9001-byte packets fail unless MTU is lowered or path MTU discovery works.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual re-establishment: not required.
• BGP can't fail over: it can.
• TGW VPN no BGP: it supports BGP.

Key takeaway: plan MTU for the backup path.

stem: A company has 20 VPCs across several accounts that all need full any-to-any IP connectivity, and the number of VPCs is expected to keep growing. Using VPC peering, this would require up to 190 individual peering connections and per-VPC route table entries for every other VPC. What architecture significantly simplifies this as the VPC count grows?

choices.text: One Direct Connect gateway per VPC on a shared DX connection
Hub-and-spoke with a Transit Gateway
A full mesh of VPC peering
One shared VPC (via RAM) for all 20 workloads instead of separate VPCs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Transit Gateway gives hub-and-spoke any-to-any connectivity that scales as VPCs grow.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DX gateway per VPC: for on-premises.
• Full mesh peering: grows as n².
• One shared VPC: loses account separation.

Key takeaway: many VPCs any-to-any → TGW.

stem: An architect is comparing VPC peering with Transit Gateway for 60 VPCs. Which TWO statements about peering are correct? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Peering isn't transitive: A-B and B-C doesn't give A-C
Peering can't be used across accounts
Each VPC has a quota on active peering connections
Peering can't be used across Regions
Peering charges an hourly fee per peering attachment, like Transit Gateway

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Peering creates direct one-to-one connections and doesn't route through an intermediary VPC, and each VPC has a limit on active peerings, so a full mesh of 60 VPCs becomes unmanageable. Transit Gateway gives hub-and-spoke routing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hourly attachment fee: that's a Transit Gateway charge; peering has no hourly fee.
• Cross-account and cross-Region: both are supported by peering.

Key takeaway: many VPCs → Transit Gateway; a few with heavy traffic → peering can be cheaper.

stem: A company wants all outbound internet traffic from dozens of spoke VPCs to egress through a single centralized set of NAT gateways in a shared services VPC, rather than deploying NAT gateways in every spoke VPC, in order to reduce cost and centralize egress monitoring. How should this be architected using Transit Gateway?

choices.text: A NAT gateway in every spoke VPC, with TGW used only for east-west traffic
Spokes route 0.0.0.0/0 to the TGW, which routes it to the egress VPC
Use VPC endpoints for all internet-bound traffic instead of NAT gateways
Peer each spoke with the shared VPC and route 0.0.0.0/0 over peering

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Spokes route 0.0.0.0/0 to the TGW, which routes it to the central egress VPC with NAT gateways (and return routes back).

Why the other options are wrong:
• NAT in every spoke: not centralized.
• VPC endpoints for internet: not possible.
• Peering for 0.0.0.0/0: peering isn't transitive for internet egress.

Key takeaway: central egress → TGW default route to egress VPC.

stem: A company must ensure that a set of VPCs handling PCI-regulated workloads can never establish direct network connectivity to a set of general-purpose VPCs, even though both sets are attached to the same Transit Gateway and occasionally need to reach a shared services VPC. How should Transit Gateway route tables be designed?

choices.text: Disable route propagation on the Transit Gateway and segment only with VPC-level network ACLs
Attach the PCI VPCs to a separate Transit Gateway and copy security group rules between them manually
Separate TGW route tables; only shared-services routes propagate to both
Use one Transit Gateway route table for all attachments and block PCI traffic with security groups alone

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Separate TGW route tables let PCI attachments learn only shared-services routes, so PCI VPCs have no route to non-PCI VPCs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable propagation without separation: doesn't isolate.
• Separate TGW copying SGs: SGs don't control TGW routing.
• One table with blocking: fragile.

Key takeaway: segmentation on TGW = route table association/propagation.

stem: VPC A and VPC B are both attached to the same Transit Gateway, but instances in VPC A cannot reach instances in VPC B despite the Transit Gateway route table showing a propagated route for VPC B's CIDR. What else must be verified to fully troubleshoot this?

choices.text: That the TGW route table uses static routes, since propagation never installs a usable route
That the Transit Gateway has multicast support enabled
That VPC A's subnet route table points VPC B's CIDR at the TGW
That both VPCs are in the same Availability Zone

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Each VPC's subnet route table must send the other VPC's CIDR to the TGW. Missing subnet routes are a common cause.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Static routes required: propagation works.
• Multicast: unrelated.
• Same AZ: not required.

Key takeaway: TGW needs routes in VPC and TGW route tables.

stem: A company deploys a centralized inspection VPC with a Gateway Load Balancer and stateful firewall appliances to inspect east-west traffic between spoke VPCs, all connected through a Transit Gateway. Testing reveals that some flows between two spoke VPCs are being dropped by the firewall because outbound and return traffic for the same flow are inspected by different firewall appliance instances in different Availability Zones. What should be enabled to fix this for VPC-to-VPC (east-west) inspection through Transit Gateway?

choices.text: Appliance mode on the inspection VPC attachment
Multicast support on the Transit Gateway
A second Transit Gateway only for return traffic
Cross-zone load balancing on the Transit Gateway

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Appliance mode on the inspection VPC attachment keeps flows symmetric through the same AZ and appliance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Multicast: unrelated.
• Second TGW: unnecessary.
• Cross-zone on TGW: not a setting.

Key takeaway: stateful inspection + TGW → appliance mode.

stem: Two Transit Gateways in different Regions, each with their own set of attached VPCs, need to exchange routes so that VPCs attached to one can reach VPCs attached to the other, without traffic traversing the public internet. Which approach should be used, and what routing limitation applies?

choices.text: VPC peering between VPCs in both Regions instead of Transit Gateway peering
AWS PrivateLink between the two Transit Gateways
TGW peering, with routes propagated automatically like any VPC attachment
A TGW peering attachment, with static routes added (no propagation over peering)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
TGW peering attachments don't support route propagation. Add static routes pointing to the peering attachment in each TGW's route table.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPC peering instead: loses hub model.
• PrivateLink between TGWs: no.
• Automatic propagation: not supported.

Key takeaway: TGW peering = static routes.

stem: A media processing company needs to send the same video stream from a single source instance to multiple receiver instances across several VPCs attached to the same Transit Gateway, using IP multicast rather than replicating unicast streams to each receiver individually. Which Transit Gateway feature supports this?

choices.text: Transit Gateway Connect attachments
Transit Gateway multicast domains (IGMPv2 or static)
Transit Gateway peering with broadcast mode enabled
VPC Flow Logs configured with a multicast filter

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transit Gateway multicast domains deliver one stream to multiple receivers (IGMPv2 or static membership).

Why the other options are wrong:
• TGW Connect: SD-WAN.
• Broadcast mode peering: doesn't exist.
• Flow log filter: logging.

Key takeaway: multicast on AWS → TGW multicast.

stem: A network account owns a Transit Gateway that 30 accounts must attach to, and attachments should be accepted automatically only from the organization. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Copy the TGW configuration into each account with StackSets
Share via RAM within the org; accounts create attachments
Create all attachments centrally by assuming roles into each account
Enable a TGW delegated administrator to attach all VPCs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS RAM shares the TGW with the organization, so member accounts can create their own VPC attachments. The owner can enable auto-accept for shared attachments.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Central attachments via roles: heavy and centralizes work unnecessarily.
• Copying config: creates separate TGWs.
• Delegated admin auto-attach: not how TGW sharing works.

Key takeaway: shared network resources → RAM.

stem: A company wants MACsec on a new Direct Connect link later. Which choices at provisioning time keep this option open?

choices.text: A 1 Gbps dedicated connection at any location, upgraded to MACsec later
Any hosted connection, then enable MACsec later
MACsec is enabled automatically on LAGs
Dedicated 10/100/400 Gbps at a MACsec-capable location

explanation:
Why this is correct:
MACsec is supported on dedicated connections at eligible speeds (10, 100, 400 Gbps) on MACsec-capable devices, so these choices must be made at order time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hosted connections: don't support MACsec.
• 1 Gbps: not an eligible speed.
• Automatic on LAGs: it must be configured with keys.

Key takeaway: MACsec = dedicated + eligible speed + capable location.

stem: A company has a 100 Gbps Direct Connect LAG composed of two 100 Gbps dedicated connections at a MACsec-capable location and wants to enable MACsec encryption across the LAG. Which requirement must be satisfied?

choices.text: LAG members share a single MACsec session negotiated at the LAG level
Only one member needs a CKN/CAK pair
Each member needs its own CKN/CAK association
MACsec requires recreating the members as hosted connections first

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Each LAG member connection needs its own MACsec CKN/CAK association.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shared session at LAG level: no.
• One member only: all members need keys.
• Hosted connections: MACsec is for dedicated.

Key takeaway: MACsec keys per member.

stem: After enabling MACsec "must secure" mode on one member connection of a two-member Direct Connect LAG, traffic across that member drops to zero while the other member continues to pass traffic normally, and BGP is up on both connections. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: MACsec cannot be enabled per member, so this configuration is not possible
The LAG minimum links threshold was not met
The other member draws all traffic because of BGP local preference
The router's CKN/CAK doesn't match AWS, so must-secure blocks traffic

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With must-secure mode, traffic flows only if MACsec is established. A CKN/CAK mismatch between the router and AWS blocks traffic on that member.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't enable per member: you can.
• Minimum links: would affect the whole LAG.
• BGP local preference: not member-level.

Key takeaway: must-secure + key mismatch = no traffic.

stem: A company has two Direct Connect connections at two different Direct Connect locations, both advertising the same on-premises prefix to AWS via BGP. They want AWS-to-on-premises traffic to prefer Connection A and use Connection B only as backup. Which action on the on-premises routers achieves this using AS path manipulation?

choices.text: Set a lower MED on the routes advertised over Connection A
Prepend the AS path on routes advertised from on-premises over Connection B
Raise local preference on routes received from Connection B
Prepend the AS path on routes advertised from AWS over Connection A

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Prepending the AS path on routes advertised from on-premises over Connection B makes AWS prefer Connection A for return traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lower MED on A: MED isn't compared across different locations reliably.
• Local preference on B: affects on-prem outbound.
• Prepend from AWS: you don't control AWS advertisements.

Key takeaway: steer AWS→on-prem traffic by prepending your advertisements.

stem: An enterprise has two Direct Connect private VIFs terminating in the same AWS Region from two different on-premises routers, both advertising the same on-premises prefix. They want AWS to consistently prefer routes from VIF A over VIF B without changing AS path length. Which approach is correct per AWS Direct Connect's supported BGP mechanisms?

choices.text: Set a higher MED on routes over VIF A
Tag VIF B routes with the low local-preference community
Open a support case to have AWS adjust local preference for the customer's ASN
A static route on the AWS side with a higher administrative distance for VIF B

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS supports BGP local preference communities. Tagging VIF B routes with the low local-preference community makes AWS prefer VIF A.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Higher MED on A: makes A less preferred.
• Support case: not needed.
• Static route with admin distance: not available.

Key takeaway: control AWS path selection with communities.

stem: An enterprise advertises the same on-premises prefix over two separate Direct Connect private VIFs from two different customer routers using two different customer ASNs (one is a backup connection from a secondary data center), and sets a lower MED on the primary path's advertisement. However, AWS continues to send traffic to the backup path more often than expected. What explains this?

choices.text: The backup route was learned via iBGP, so it's preferred over the primary eBGP route
MED values must be higher, not lower, to be preferred by AWS
Direct Connect does not support MED on any virtual interface type
MED is compared only between routes from the same neighboring AS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
MED is compared only between routes from the same neighboring AS. If the paths come from different ASNs, MED doesn't influence selection.

Why the other options are wrong:
• iBGP preference: not the case.
• Higher MED preferred: lower is preferred.
• No MED support: MED is supported.

Key takeaway: MED works within one neighbor AS.

stem: A customer's on-premises router receives the same VPC prefix from AWS over two Direct Connect private VIFs: one path has a shorter AS path but the administrator manually set a lower local preference for it, while the other path has a longer AS path but a higher local preference. Which path does standard BGP best path selection choose?

choices.text: The higher local preference path (evaluated before AS path)
Both paths are installed and load-balanced
The shorter AS path, since AS path length is evaluated before local preference
Neither until MED is compared, since MED precedes local preference

explanation:
Why this is correct:
On the customer router, higher local preference wins before AS path length, so that path is chosen.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both installed: not by default.
• AS path first: local preference comes before.
• MED first: MED comes later.

Key takeaway: BGP order: local preference → AS path → MED.

stem: A branch router doesn't support BGP. It connects with Site-to-Site VPN to a VGW. What must be configured, and how does failover between the two tunnels work?

choices.text: Static routes; failover depends on the device detecting tunnel state
Policy-based VPN, since routing options don't apply
Static routing, with AWS failing over automatically via BGP withdrawal
BGP, since static routing isn't supported

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Without BGP, the VPN uses static routes that list on-premises prefixes. There's no route withdrawal, so the customer device must detect a down tunnel (for example, with DPD) and use the other.

Why the other options are wrong:
• BGP required: static routing is supported.
• Automatic BGP withdrawal: there's no BGP.
• Policy-based only: static routing still applies.

Key takeaway: static VPN = manual prefixes + device-driven failover.

stem: A Site-to-Site VPN connection using BGP dynamic routing has two tunnels, both showing UP status. During a planned maintenance test, the customer shuts down the primary tunnel's IPsec session on their firewall, but traffic does not fail over to the second tunnel for several minutes, causing an outage. What is the most likely root cause?

choices.text: Site-to-Site VPN doesn't support two tunnels being BGP-active at once
The customer gateway isn't withdrawing the dead tunnel's route promptly
Both tunnels must terminate on the same on-premises device for failover
Propagated VPC routes can't fail over without manual intervention

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If traffic doesn't fail over, the customer gateway may keep advertising routes over the dead tunnel. The device must withdraw them (for example, by detecting the tunnel down).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Two active tunnels unsupported: supported.
• Same device required: no.
• Propagated routes need manual action: no.

Key takeaway: failover requires route withdrawal.

stem: A financial services company is deciding between static routing and BGP dynamic routing for a new Site-to-Site VPN that will back up an existing Direct Connect connection, and they plan to add and remove VPC CIDR ranges frequently as new workloads are deployed. Which tradeoff should most influence their decision toward BGP?

choices.text: BGP propagates prefix changes without manual route updates
BGP is required for AES-256 on the tunnels, while static routing is limited to AES-128
Static routing has lower per-packet latency
BGP is the only option that supports ECMP across both tunnels of one connection

explanation:
Why this is correct:
BGP propagates prefix changes automatically, without manual route updates on either side.

Why the other options are wrong:
• BGP needed for AES-256: no.
• Static lower latency: no.
• BGP only option for ECMP: not the key difference asked.

Key takeaway: dynamic routing reduces manual changes.

stem: A healthcare company requires Direct Connect connectivity that can tolerate the failure of an entire Direct Connect location without manual intervention, and wants to meet AWS's defined resiliency model for that use case with the fewest connections possible. Which resiliency model should they choose?

choices.text: Development and Test model: one connection at one location
A single Direct Connect connection using a LAG of two physical links at one location
High Resiliency model: one connection at each of two different Direct Connect locations
Maximum Resiliency model: two connections at each of two different Direct Connect locations (four connections total)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The High Resiliency model uses one connection at each of two DX locations, surviving a location failure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Dev/test: single location.
• LAG at one location: single location.
• Maximum Resiliency: works, but costs more than needed for the requirement.

Key takeaway: tolerate location failure → two locations.

stem: A company believed it had implemented AWS's Maximum Resiliency model for Direct Connect by provisioning two connections, but an audit reveals both connections terminate on the same device at the same location through two separate ports. During a maintenance event on that device, both connections go down simultaneously. What was misconfigured relative to the Maximum Resiliency model?

choices.text: The connections should have been combined into a single LAG
The issue is unrelated to the model and comes from BGP misconfiguration
It needs separate devices at separate locations, not two ports on one device
It only needs two customer router interfaces, regardless of AWS termination

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Maximum Resiliency requires separate connections on separate devices at separate locations, not two ports on one device.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Combine into LAG: still one device.
• BGP issue: not the design gap.
• Only two router interfaces: ignores AWS side.

Key takeaway: resiliency depends on device and location diversity.

stem: How does the AWS Direct Connect Maximum Resiliency model differ from the High Resiliency model in terms of failure protection?

choices.text: Maximum protects only against device failure; High only against location failure
Maximum uses one connection at four locations; High uses four at one location
High survives a location loss; Maximum also survives a device loss per location
No difference; Maximum Resiliency is a marketing name for High Resiliency

explanation:
Why this is correct:
High Resiliency survives a location loss. Maximum Resiliency adds device redundancy within each location, surviving device failures too.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Swapped protections: incorrect.
• Location counts wrong: incorrect.
• Same thing: different.

Key takeaway: Maximum = High + device redundancy.

stem: A company routes all outbound internet traffic from multiple spoke VPCs through a centralized inspection VPC containing third-party firewall appliances behind a Gateway Load Balancer, all connected via Transit Gateway. Spoke VPCs send 0.0.0.0/0 to the TGW, which forwards it to the inspection VPC before it exits via an IGW or NAT gateway. Which Transit Gateway feature must be enabled on the inspection VPC's attachment to avoid asymmetric routing through the stateful appliances?

choices.text: Transit Gateway Connect
Jumbo frame support (MTU 8500)
Appliance mode
Multicast support

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Appliance mode keeps return traffic on the same AZ and inspection appliance for centralized egress through a TGW.

Why the other options are wrong:
• TGW Connect: SD-WAN.
• Jumbo frames: MTU.
• Multicast: unrelated.

Key takeaway: symmetric inspection → appliance mode.

stem: A newly created VPC attachment to a Transit Gateway is active, and the VPC's route table correctly points 10.0.0.0/8 to the TGW. However, resources in that VPC cannot reach another VPC attached to the same TGW, and the second VPC's CIDR does not appear in the TGW route table associated with the first VPC's attachment. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: Missing route table association or propagation for the new attachment
TGW route tables refresh only once every 24 hours
The second VPC's security group blocks the route from propagating
Transit Gateway can't route VPC-to-VPC without a Direct Connect gateway

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A new attachment needs a TGW route table association and propagation (or static routes) so other VPCs learn its CIDR.

Why the other options are wrong:
• 24-hour refresh: false.
• SG blocks propagation: SGs don't affect routes.
• DX required: false.

Key takeaway: TGW routes need association and propagation.

stem: A media company needs to distribute a live video feed to EC2 instances across several VPCs using IP multicast instead of replicating unicast streams to each subscriber. Which AWS capability directly supports this, and what is a key design constraint?

choices.text: TGW multicast; only same-TGW VPCs with associated subnets
Elastic Load Balancing, which supports multicast to targets across VPCs
A Route 53 multicast routing policy, limited to private hosted zones
VPC peering multicast, although multicast isn't supported over peering

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transit Gateway multicast delivers to receivers in VPCs attached to the same TGW whose subnets are associated with the multicast domain.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ELB multicast: not supported.
• Route 53 multicast: doesn't exist.
• Peering multicast: not supported.

Key takeaway: multicast scope = same TGW, associated subnets.

stem: A global enterprise needs VPCs in ap-northeast-2 and eu-west-1 to connect to a shared set of VPCs, and also wants a single Direct Connect connection in us-east-1 to reach VPCs in all three Regions without deploying Direct Connect in each Region. Which combination of design choices is correct?

choices.text: Inter-Region TGW peering, plus a DX gateway associated with each Region's TGW
VPC peering across Regions, since TGW peering doesn't support inter-Region links
A DX gateway associates only with a same-Region TGW
TGW peering propagates DX gateway routes to peered TGWs with no route table changes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inter-Region TGW peering connects Regions, and a DX gateway associated with each Region's TGW gives on-premises access (TGW peering doesn't propagate DX routes).

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPC peering because TGW can't: TGW peering supports inter-Region.
• DX gateway only same Region: it associates across Regions.
• Automatic DX route propagation over peering: no.

Key takeaway: combine TGW peering with DX gateway associations.

stem: A SaaS provider runs its service behind a Network Load Balancer in its own VPC and wants customer VPCs in other AWS accounts to privately consume the service without VPC peering, without traffic ever traversing the public internet, and while retaining full control over which consumer accounts can connect. Which architecture should they implement?

choices.text: A gateway VPC endpoint for the NLB, shared to consumer accounts through AWS RAM
An NLB-backed endpoint service with consumer interface endpoints
A public ALB restricted by security groups to each customer's NAT gateway IP
VPC peering with every consumer VPC, advertising the NLB's private IP over BGP

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An NLB-backed endpoint service lets consumer VPCs create interface endpoints, exposing only the service privately.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Gateway endpoint for an NLB: gateway endpoints are only for S3 and DynamoDB.
• Public ALB: internet exposure.
• Peering with every consumer: exposes networks.

Key takeaway: private SaaS exposure → PrivateLink.

stem: A consumer account created an Interface VPC Endpoint for a partner's endpoint service, which shows Available status. However, applications referencing the service's standard public DNS name (service.partner.com) still resolve to a public IP and bypass the endpoint. What is the most likely misconfiguration?

choices.text: Private DNS isn't enabled or the service lacks a verified private DNS name
The endpoint ENIs' security group is blocking DNS traffic on port 53
Endpoints never override public DNS, so apps must hardcode the private IPs
The endpoint service must be recreated as a Gateway endpoint for private DNS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clients use the public name only if private DNS is enabled on the endpoint and the service has a verified private DNS name.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SG blocks DNS: DNS isn't through the endpoint SG.
• Endpoints never override DNS: private DNS does.
• Recreate as gateway endpoint: not possible.

Key takeaway: private DNS makes endpoints transparent.

stem: A security team wants to insert a third-party virtual appliance transparently in the traffic path between many VPCs and the internet, without applications needing to change their target endpoints, and wants the appliance fleet reusable across many VPCs and accounts. Which PrivateLink-based approach fits, and what is the key distinction versus a standard Interface Endpoint to an NLB-backed service?

choices.text: GWLB can't be exposed through PrivateLink and works only within one VPC
A Gateway Load Balancer endpoint for transparent inline inspection
A gateway VPC endpoint, since GWLB requires gateway-type endpoints
A standard interface endpoint to the GWLB, identical to one for an NLB

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Gateway Load Balancer endpoint (a PrivateLink endpoint type) inserts the appliance transparently in the traffic path through route tables.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GWLB can't use PrivateLink: it does via GWLB endpoints.
• Gateway VPC endpoint: only S3/DynamoDB.
• Standard interface endpoint: not inline routing.

Key takeaway: transparent inline inspection → GWLB endpoint.

stem: A central networking team manages shared subnets in a networking account and wants application teams in dozens of other accounts within the same Organization to launch EC2 instances directly into those subnets, while the networking team retains ownership of the VPC and subnet resources. Which approach satisfies this?

choices.text: VPC peering between the networking VPC and each application VPC
Cross-account roles to launch into the networking account
Share the subnets with the application accounts through AWS RAM
Copy the subnet CIDRs into each account's VPC with StackSets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
VPC sharing through AWS RAM lets application accounts launch resources into centrally managed subnets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Peering: separate VPCs.
• Roles into the networking account: resources land in the wrong account.
• Copying CIDRs: creates separate, possibly overlapping VPCs.

Key takeaway: central subnets for many accounts → RAM sharing.

stem: After a subnet is shared via AWS RAM with a participant account, a developer there attempts to launch an EC2 instance into the shared subnet but receives an authorization error, even though the resource share shows Active and was accepted. What should be checked first?

choices.text: Whether the subnet was shared read-only, since shared subnets are always read-only
Whether the developer's IAM identity has ec2:RunInstances permissions
Whether the VPC has enableDnsSupport, required before RAM sharing
Whether both accounts are in the same Region, since RAM can't share across Regions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Participants still need IAM permissions (such as ec2:RunInstances) in their own account to launch into shared subnets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Read-only shares: subnet shares aren't read-only.
• DNS attribute needed for sharing: no.
• Same Region: shares are Regional, but that's not the likely cause.

Key takeaway: shared subnets still need participant IAM.

stem: A company wants to share a Transit Gateway created in a central network account with 40 accounts spanning two different AWS Organizations after an acquisition, so all accounts can create attachments to it. What is a key constraint they must design around when using AWS RAM?

choices.text: Within an org, sharing can be automatic; across orgs, specify account IDs and accept invitations
The two Organizations must be merged before any RAM share can be created
Cross-organization RAM sharing is impossible, so a separate TGW is needed
Transit Gateways can't be shared via RAM; only subnets support sharing

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Within an organization, RAM sharing can be automatic (no invitations). Accounts outside it must be specified individually and accept invitations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Merge orgs: not required.
• Cross-org impossible: possible with invitations.
• TGWs can't be shared: they can.

Key takeaway: RAM: org sharing is seamless; external needs invitations.

stem: A company operating in three AWS Regions wants to prevent CIDR overlap as dozens of teams create new VPCs, while still letting each Region's network team allocate specific ranges within their Region's overall pool. Which IPAM design achieves this?

choices.text: A top-level pool with Regional child pools delegated per team
IPAM supports a single global pool
One flat pool per team with no hierarchy, tracking overlaps in a spreadsheet
Separate IPAM instances per Region with no shared pool, avoiding overlap by convention

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An IPAM hierarchy with a top-level pool and Regional child pools delegated to teams allocates non-overlapping CIDRs everywhere.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Single global pool only: hierarchies are supported.
• Flat pools per team: overlaps possible.
• Separate IPAMs per Region: no global view.

Key takeaway: org-wide addressing → IPAM pool hierarchy.

stem: A company using IPAM discovers that a newly onboarded account created a VPC whose CIDR overlaps with an existing VPC in another account, even though both accounts are integrated with the same IPAM. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: IPAM allows overlaps up to a /24 by design to support future subnetting
Overlap prevention works only across separate Organizations, not within one
The CIDR was set manually, not allocated from the pool
IPAM doesn't check overlaps; it only provides inventory and reporting

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IPAM prevents overlap only for CIDRs allocated from its pools. A manually specified CIDR can overlap; IPAM will flag it for monitoring.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Allows /24 overlaps: no.
• Only across orgs: no.
• No overlap checks: it checks pool allocations.

Key takeaway: enforce allocation from IPAM pools.

stem: A company has brought its own public IPv4 range to AWS using BYOIP and wants to manage allocation of smaller blocks from that range to individual accounts for use with Elastic IPs and NLBs, tracking utilization centrally. What is the appropriate way to integrate this BYOIP range with IPAM, and what limitation applies?

choices.text: BYOIP ranges import into IPAM automatically once announced via BGP
IPAM can't manage public IP space; it's limited to RFC 1918 ranges
The BYOIP range must be converted to private IP space before tracking
After BYOIP onboarding, provision it into a public-scope IPAM pool

explanation:
Why this is correct:
