After BYOIP onboarding, provision the range into a public-scope IPAM pool to manage allocations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Automatic import: not automatic.
• IPAM only private: it has a public scope.
• Convert to private: no.

Key takeaway: BYOIP management → public-scope IPAM pools.

stem: VPCs must resolve corp.example.internal via on-premises DNS over Direct Connect, and on-premises must resolve a private hosted zone. Which components fit?

choices.text: No endpoints; DNS flows over the VPN automatically
A public hosted zone with NS records to on-premises
Outbound endpoint + forwarding rule; inbound endpoint for on-prem
An inbound endpoint only, with a private hosted zone

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Outbound endpoints with forwarding rules send VPC queries for on-premises domains to on-premises DNS. Inbound endpoints receive queries from on-premises for private hosted zones.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inbound only: covers on-prem-to-AWS but not the reverse.
• Public zone: exposes internal names.
• Automatic flow: the VPC resolver doesn't forward on its own.

Key takeaway: AWS → on-prem = outbound; on-prem → AWS = inbound.

stem: A VPC has two Resolver forwarding rules: one for example.internal targeting on-premises DNS servers, and a more specific rule for db.example.internal targeting a partner network. A query for app.db.example.internal unexpectedly receives answers from the on-premises servers configured for example.internal instead. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: Resolver applies rules alphabetically, regardless of domain specificity
Forwarding rules support only single-label domains, so this one is invalid
Rules can't overlap as parent/child domains
The more specific rule isn't associated with that VPC

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Resolver uses the most specific matching rule associated with the VPC. If the more specific rule isn't associated with that VPC, the broader rule applies.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Alphabetical: no.
• Single-label only: no.
• No parent/child overlap: allowed.

Key takeaway: most specific associated rule wins.

stem: A VPC has a DNS Firewall rule group blocking known-malicious domains, and a separate conditional forwarding rule sending queries for internal.example.com to an on-premises DNS server. A query is issued for a domain that matches both the DNS Firewall block list and is a subdomain of internal.example.com. What determines the outcome, and why does this matter operationally?

choices.text: DNS Firewall inspects only internet-bound queries, never forwarded domains
The query fails with SERVFAIL
DNS Firewall can still block it despite the forwarding rule
Forwarding rules always take priority, so the query goes on-premises unfiltered

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DNS Firewall evaluates queries from the VPC before forwarding, so a blocked domain is blocked even if a forwarding rule exists.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only internet-bound: it filters all Resolver queries.
• SERVFAIL always: depends on the block response configured.
• Forwarding always wins: no.

Key takeaway: DNS Firewall applies before forwarding.

stem: An on-premises application needs to resolve names hosted in a private hosted zone associated with a VPC in AWS, with queries originating on-premises traveling over an existing Direct Connect connection. Which Route 53 Resolver component must be deployed to allow this?

choices.text: A Resolver outbound endpoint
AWS Directory Service, since Resolver doesn't support hybrid resolution
A public hosted zone duplicating the private zone's records
An inbound endpoint, with on-prem DNS forwarding to it

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An inbound Resolver endpoint accepts queries from on-premises DNS servers configured to forward the zone to it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Outbound endpoint: VPC to on-premises.
• Directory Service: not required.
• Public zone duplicate: exposes names.

Key takeaway: on-prem resolving private zones → inbound endpoint.

stem: A Resolver rule for corp.internal was shared from a networking account to a spoke account via RAM, and the invitation was accepted. However, associating the rule with a VPC in the spoke account is not available in the console. What is a likely cause?

choices.text: The spoke must be in the rule targets' Region; cross-Region sharing is never possible
The principal lacks route53resolver:AssociateResolverRule
Cross-account sharing works only for inbound-endpoint rules, not forwarding rules
Shared rules can be associated only via the CLI, never through the console

explanation:
Why this is correct:
After a rule is shared, the spoke account's principal needs route53resolver:AssociateResolverRule permission to associate it with a VPC.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cross-Region limitation: not the cause.
• Only inbound rules: forwarding rules share fine.
• CLI only: console works too.

Key takeaway: sharing isn't enough; associating needs IAM.

stem: A large enterprise with 60 AWS accounts wants a centralized hybrid DNS architecture where all VPCs can resolve on-premises names and on-premises clients can resolve AWS private hosted zone names, while minimizing the number of Resolver endpoints deployed and the operational overhead of managing rules across accounts. Which architecture best achieves this?

choices.text: Use only public hosted zones for internal names to avoid endpoints and forwarding
A separate pair of inbound and outbound endpoints in every one of the 60 accounts
Resolver endpoints can't be centralized; each VPC needs its own endpoints and rules
Central endpoints and rules in a DNS account, shared via RAM

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Central inbound and outbound endpoints and forwarding rules in a DNS account, shared through RAM and associated with all VPCs, provide hybrid DNS without per-VPC endpoints.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public zones: expose names.
• Endpoints per VPC: costly.
• Can't centralize: they can.

Key takeaway: centralize hybrid DNS in one account.

stem: A company wants internal clients inside their VPCs to resolve www.example.com to an internal ALB's private IP, while external internet clients continue resolving the same name to a public-facing CloudFront distribution. Which Route 53 design achieves this split-horizon behavior, and what operational tradeoff does it introduce?

choices.text: Split-horizon DNS isn't possible in Route 53, so a different internal domain is needed
One hosted zone with geolocation routing to tell VPC queries from internet queries
Enable VPC-only mode on the public zone to hide internal records from outside
A private zone of the same name for the VPCs; shared records must be synced manually

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A private hosted zone with the same name as the public zone gives VPC clients internal answers (split-horizon). Records needed in both must exist in both zones.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Split-horizon impossible: it's supported.
• Geolocation for VPC vs. public: not how it works.
• VPC-only mode on public zone: doesn't exist.

Key takeaway: split-horizon → same-name private + public zones.

stem: Instances must not resolve malware C2 domains, using AWS-maintained lists, while a partner domain wrongly flagged must stay allowed. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: NACLs denying the IP ranges published for known C2 infrastructure
DNS Firewall: ALLOW rule for the partner first, then managed BLOCK list
Security groups blocking outbound port 53
GuardDuty DNS findings as the blocking mechanism

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DNS Firewall evaluates rules by priority. A higher-priority ALLOW rule for the partner domain, followed by a BLOCK rule using the AWS managed malware list, handles the exception.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SG port 53: blocks all DNS, not specific domains.
• NACL IP ranges: C2 IPs change; not domain-based.
• GuardDuty: detects, doesn't block.

Key takeaway: domain blocking with exceptions → DNS Firewall rule priority.

stem: A security architect is deciding whether to enforce domain-based outbound restrictions using Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall, AWS Network Firewall's domain filtering, or both together. Which statement correctly describes the distinction and the rationale for combining them?

choices.text: DNS Firewall blocks resolution; Network Firewall inspects flows (SNI); together they add depth
Network Firewall can't filter by domain; it's limited to 5-tuple IP and port rules
DNS Firewall inspects TLS SNI, making Network Firewall's domain filtering redundant
They are functionally identical, so deploying both adds no security benefit

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DNS Firewall blocks resolution of disallowed domains. Network Firewall inspects actual flows (SNI, HTTP host), catching direct-IP connections too. They complement each other.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Network Firewall can't filter domains: it can.
• DNS Firewall inspects SNI: it doesn't.
• Identical: different layers.

Key takeaway: DNS layer vs. traffic layer.

stem: A network team must deploy the same Transit Gateway route tables and VPC attachments to 40 accounts and 3 Regions, with drift detection. Which approach fits?

choices.text: EventBridge schedules calling EC2 APIs
Manual console setup with a runbook
AWS Config rules that create missing resources
CloudFormation StackSets with TGW resource types

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFormation declares TGW resources such as route tables, attachments, and associations, and StackSets deploys them across accounts and Regions, with drift detection on stack instances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config rules: evaluate compliance, not provisioning.
• Scheduled API scripts: imperative, with no drift detection.
• Manual setup: inconsistent at this scale.

Key takeaway: multi-account IaC → StackSets.

stem: A CloudFormation stack update that adds a new route to an existing VPC route table fails and rolls back with an error that the route already exists with a different target. Investigation shows a network engineer manually added an identical-looking route directly in the console outside CloudFormation. What behavior explains this failure, and what is the recommended remediation?

choices.text: Route tables are immutable in CloudFormation
Drift from the manual route; detect drift, then import or remove it
It's unrelated to the manual change and caused by too many subnet associations
CloudFormation overwrites conflicting manual resources, so this is a service failure

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A manual route matching the new route causes a conflict. Detect drift, then import or remove the manual route so CloudFormation can manage it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route tables immutable: no.
• Too many subnets: unrelated.
• CFN overwrites: it fails instead.

Key takeaway: manual changes cause stack conflicts.

stem: A platform team is building a reusable component in AWS CDK that provisions a Transit Gateway attachment for any VPC stack across the organization, and wants application teams to consume this logic without understanding the underlying CloudFormation resource details. Which CDK concept should they use?

choices.text: A custom CDK construct with a typed props interface
A nested stack written in raw JSON
Config conformance packs, the CDK-native way to share infrastructure logic
A Parameter Store value with raw CloudFormation YAML that stacks copy and paste

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A custom CDK construct with a typed props interface packages the attachment logic for reuse with validation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Raw JSON nested stack: less reusable.
• Conformance packs: compliance.
• YAML in Parameter Store: hacky.

Key takeaway: reusable infrastructure components → CDK constructs.

stem: A company needs to deploy an identical baseline of networking resources (a Transit Gateway attachment, route table entries, and VPC endpoint configuration) to 150 accounts across an Organization, with new accounts automatically receiving the baseline and central visibility into deployment status. What is the most appropriate mechanism, and what tradeoff does it involve compared to deploying stacks manually in each account?

choices.text: Config aggregators can deploy CloudFormation resources across accounts, replacing StackSets
Service-managed StackSets auto-deploy to new OU accounts, adding operational complexity
StackSets can't target OUs, so each account ID must be listed and updated manually
Deploying the template by hand in 150 accounts is just as efficient and automatic

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Service-managed StackSets targeting OUs automatically deploy the baseline to new accounts added to them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config aggregators deploy: no.
• Can't target OUs: service-managed can.
• Manual in 150 accounts: toil.

Key takeaway: OU-wide baseline → service-managed StackSets.

stem: The NOC wants one topology view of TGWs in 4 Regions, on-premises sites, SD-WAN devices, and link health, plus route analysis between two endpoints. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Config advanced queries
AWS Network Manager with a global network and Route Analyzer
Trusted Advisor network checks
CloudWatch Synthetics canaries probing each site and Region

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Network Manager provides a global network view that registers TGWs, sites, devices, and links, visualizes topology and health, and its Route Analyzer checks paths between endpoints.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config queries: resource configuration, with no topology view.
• Trusted Advisor: best-practice checks.
• Synthetics: endpoint tests, not topology.

Key takeaway: global network topology → Network Manager.

stem: A network operations team uses Network Manager's global network to monitor a hybrid environment where branch offices connect via SD-WAN appliances establishing Transit Gateway Connect attachments. They want to correlate the health of the on-premises links with the AWS-side Transit Gateway attachments in one place. Which Network Manager capability supports this?

choices.text: SD-WAN integration requires a separate service called AWS SD-WAN Manager
Connect attachments are invisible to Network Manager and need VPC Flow Logs instead
Network Manager monitors only attachments and has no concept of sites or devices
Register SD-WAN sites, links, and devices in the global network

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Register SD-WAN sites, links, and devices in the global network so Network Manager shows them alongside Connect attachments.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Separate SD-WAN service: no.
• Connect attachments invisible: no.
• No site concept: it has sites.

Key takeaway: model on-prem topology in the global network.

stem: A network engineer notices a Direct Connect connection registered in AWS Network Manager's global network shows as Down, but the Direct Connect console shows the same connection's BGP state as Up with traffic flowing normally. What is a plausible explanation for this discrepancy?

choices.text: The Direct Connect console is malfunctioning
Network Manager uses event data and metrics that can lag live BGP state
BGP and physical state are the same value, so this indicates data corruption
Network Manager cannot register or display Direct Connect connection status

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Network Manager relies on event data and metrics that can lag live state. Confirm current status in the Direct Connect console or router.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Console malfunctioning: unlikely.
• Same value means disconnect: no.
• Can't display DX: it can.

Key takeaway: monitoring views may lag.

stem: A security team wants to automatically detect when a security group is modified to allow inbound traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22, and immediately revert the offending rule without waiting for a scheduled compliance scan. Which combination of services implements this as automated, event-driven remediation?

choices.text: EventBridge on AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress triggering a revoking Lambda
Amazon GuardDuty, which modifies security groups directly to remediate findings
Amazon Inspector, which revokes non-compliant rules the moment they are created
A daily AWS Config rule that only reports non-compliant groups with no action

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule on AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress (via CloudTrail) triggers a Lambda that revokes the offending rule within seconds.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GuardDuty modifies SGs: no.
• Inspector revokes rules: no.
• Daily Config report: slow and no remediation.

Key takeaway: real-time SG remediation → EventBridge + Lambda.

stem: A Lambda function intended to automatically remediate overly permissive Network ACL rules is triggered correctly by an EventBridge rule, but its call to ec2:ReplaceNetworkAclEntry fails with access denied. The function's execution role includes the AWS managed ReadOnlyAccess policy. What is the fix?

choices.text: Move the function into the target VPC
Increase the function's memory, since access denied errors often come from low memory
Grant the role the needed write actions (e.g., ec2:ReplaceNetworkAclEntry)
Enable Lambda VPC access, which grants full EC2 write permissions automatically

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AccessDenied means the execution role lacks the needed write actions, such as ec2:ReplaceNetworkAclEntry.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Move into VPC: unrelated to IAM.
• More memory: unrelated.
• VPC access grants EC2 writes: no.

Key takeaway: AccessDenied → add the specific permissions.

stem: An organization wants to enforce and automatically remediate security group and NACL compliance consistently across 200 accounts, with minimal custom code to maintain, and is deciding between a custom AWS Config rule plus Lambda-based Systems Manager Automation remediation pipeline versus adopting AWS Firewall Manager. What tradeoff should drive this decision?

choices.text: No meaningful difference; both need the same custom code and policy types
Config and Lambda can't be combined; only SSM documents support remediation
Firewall Manager: central, less code; custom pipeline: more flexible, more upkeep
Firewall Manager only creates findings and can't remediate, so Lambda is required

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Firewall Manager centrally enforces and remediates SG and NACL policies with little code. A custom Config and Lambda pipeline offers more flexibility at more effort.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No difference: they differ.
• Can't combine Config and Lambda: they can.
• Firewall Manager can't remediate: it can.

Key takeaway: managed policy enforcement vs. custom flexibility.

stem: The NOC needs a safe, auditable procedure to reset a DX BGP session: check health, require approval, act, and verify, run by humans or by an alarm. Which fits?

choices.text: An SSM Automation runbook with an approval step
A Lambda function with a sleep for approval
A CloudWatch alarm action that resets BGP
An AWS Config remediation action that runs without any approval step

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Automation runbooks define multi-step procedures, including aws:approve steps, API actions, and checks, with execution history for audit. They can be started manually or by EventBridge.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda sleeping: time-limited and not auditable as a procedure.
• Config remediation: no approval here, and not suited to this operation.
• Alarm actions: limited to specific actions such as SNS or Auto Scaling.

Key takeaway: auditable, gated operations → Automation runbooks.

stem: An organization wants to automate resetting a Direct Connect BGP session for a specific virtual interface across any of 30 accounts, triggered centrally from the network operations account, without granting the central automation broad standing access to every account. Which Systems Manager Automation design pattern addresses this securely?

choices.text: Give the central Automation role AdministratorAccess in all 30 accounts
Assume a scoped cross-account role with only the needed DX permissions
Automation can't work across accounts
Use Config aggregators, which can perform write actions across linked accounts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The automation should assume a scoped cross-account role that has only the needed Direct Connect permissions in each account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AdministratorAccess: over-privileged.
• Can't work cross-account: it can.
• Config aggregators write: they don't.

Key takeaway: least-privilege cross-account automation.

stem: A team is choosing between an AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook and a custom Lambda function for a network remediation task that needs to run a sequence of API calls, pause for manual approval in some cases, and be easily auditable by non-developers reading the steps. Which comparison best justifies choosing Systems Manager Automation for this task?

choices.text: Automation runbooks always run faster than Lambda because they skip invocation overhead
Lambda functions can't call AWS APIs
Automation is a strict superset of Lambda, so Lambda shouldn't be used for networking
Automation has built-in approvals and readable, auditable steps

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Automation runbooks include approval steps and readable, auditable step logs, while Lambda offers general-purpose code.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Always faster: no.
• Lambda can't call APIs: false.
• Strict superset: no.

Key takeaway: operational runbooks → Automation.

stem: A network engineer manages two AWS Direct Connect dedicated connections terminating at different Direct Connect locations, both carrying production traffic through a Direct Connect gateway to a private virtual interface. Before an upcoming disaster recovery exercise, the engineer wants to validate that traffic properly fails over to the secondary connection without physically disconnecting any fiber or opening a support case with AWS. Which approach should the engineer use to safely simulate a connection failure?

choices.text: Shut down the primary BGP session on the router and watch failover
Ask AWS Support to disable the primary connection's physical port for the test
Delete the primary VIF in the console and recreate it after the test
Change the primary VIF's MTU to 1500 to force a BGP renegotiation

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shutting down the primary BGP session on the customer router simulates a failure safely, letting you watch traffic fail over and restore it afterward.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Support disabling ports: not how testing works.
• Deleting the VIF: disruptive.
• MTU change: unrelated.

Key takeaway: test DX failover by disabling BGP on your side.

stem: A private virtual interface on a Direct Connect connection unexpectedly transitions to Down, and CloudWatch shows the BGP peer state flapping. Router logs show the DX endpoint sent a BGP NOTIFICATION message and closed the session shortly after the customer began advertising additional summarized routes from a newly migrated data center. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The Direct Connect gateway was deleted while the VIF was still attached
The customer ASN changed, which requires recreating the virtual interface
It exceeded the maximum prefixes AWS accepts on the VIF
The customer enabled BFD, which is incompatible with private VIFs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Private VIFs accept a limited number of advertised prefixes (100). Exceeding it takes the BGP session down. Summarize routes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DX gateway deleted: different symptom.
• ASN change: different issue.
• BFD incompatible: it's supported.

Key takeaway: too many prefixes → BGP session down.

stem: An organization uses a single Transit Gateway to connect a Production VPC, a Development VPC, and a Shared Services VPC hosting a proxy and directory service. Requirements: Production and Development must never reach each other; both must be able to reach Shared Services; Shared Services must be able to initiate connections to both. How should the Transit Gateway route tables and associations be configured?

choices.text: One route table associated with all three attachments, with propagation from all
One route table for all attachments plus blackhole routes for Prod and Dev CIDRs
Two route tables, each associating Shared plus one environment, propagating both
Three route tables: Prod and Dev learn Shared; Shared learns both

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Three route tables: Prod and Dev each learn only Shared routes, and Shared learns both, so Prod and Dev can't reach each other.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One table: everyone reaches everyone.
• Blackholes in one table: fragile.
• Two tables: doesn't separate cleanly.

Key takeaway: segment with separate TGW route tables.

stem: A VPN has two tunnels. The NOC wants a page when either tunnel is down for 2 minutes, and a separate critical page when both are down. Which setup fits?

choices.text: Alarms on TunnelState per tunnel, plus a composite alarm
An alarm on the Direct Connect ConnectionState metric for the link
An alarm on EC2 NetworkPacketsIn
An alarm on TGW BytesIn for the attachment

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS/VPN publishes TunnelState per tunnel (1 up, 0 down). A per-tunnel alarm catches single failures, and a composite alarm (AND) catches total loss.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DX metric: Direct Connect, not VPN.
• TGW bytes: low traffic isn't the same as a down tunnel.
• EC2 packets: unrelated.

Key takeaway: VPN health → TunnelState; combine with composite alarms.

stem: A financial services company has two Direct Connect connections configured active/active using ECMP through a Transit Gateway. During a recent fiber cut, application teams observed roughly 60-90 seconds of packet loss before traffic converged onto the surviving connection, exceeding their RTO. Standard BGP hold-timer-based detection is currently in use. What should the network team implement to reduce failure detection and convergence time?

choices.text: Enable BFD on the virtual interfaces
Switch from a DX gateway to a virtual private gateway for each VIF
Disable route propagation on the Transit Gateway route table
Increase the BGP hold timer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
BFD detects link failures in under a second, so ECMP removes a failed path quickly instead of waiting for BGP timers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VGW instead of DX gateway: unrelated.
• Disable propagation: breaks routing.
• Longer hold timer: slower detection.

Key takeaway: fast failover → BFD.

stem: A company has two Direct Connect private virtual interfaces to the same VPC: a primary 10 Gbps connection and a backup 1 Gbps connection at a different location. They want traffic from the VPC toward on-premises to always prefer the primary connection, using the backup only when the primary is unavailable, without making any AWS-side configuration changes. Which technique should be applied on the customer router advertising routes over the backup virtual interface?

choices.text: Prepend the customer ASN multiple times on routes sent over the backup connection
Increase the MED advertised over the primary connection
Configure a lower local preference on the primary connection
Advertise a more specific prefix over the backup connection

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Prepending the customer ASN on routes sent over the backup connection makes AWS prefer the primary for return traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Higher MED on primary: makes it less preferred.
• Lower local preference on primary: affects your outbound.
• More specific on backup: makes backup preferred.

Key takeaway: make backup less attractive with prepending.

stem: During an acquisition integration, a newly attached VPC uses the same 10.0.0.0/16 CIDR as an existing VPC already attached to the company's Transit Gateway. After the new attachment, engineers notice that some instances in the existing VPC can no longer reach resources they previously could, and traffic behaves unpredictably. What is the most likely explanation and the recommended remediation?

choices.text: Overlapping CIDRs in one route table aren't supported; re-IP or isolate them
TGW permits overlapping CIDRs and load-balances between them; re-IP one VPC
It's unrelated to the overlap and caused by an MTU mismatch from the new attachment
Expected behavior; TGW disambiguates identical CIDRs with longest-prefix match

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A TGW route table can't route overlapping CIDRs from two attachments. Re-IP one VPC or use NAT or PrivateLink.

Why the other options are wrong:
• TGW load-balances overlaps: no.
• MTU mismatch: unrelated.
• Expected disambiguation: no.

Key takeaway: overlapping CIDRs need translation or re-IP.

stem: A Site-to-Site VPN tunnel intermittently drops and re-establishes every 20-30 minutes, but the on-premises firewall logs show nothing unusual. The network engineer wants visibility into the IKE and IPsec negotiation phases from the AWS side to determine whether AWS is initiating the rekey or teardown. What should be enabled to get this visibility?

choices.text: AWS CloudTrail data events for the VPN connection
Traffic Mirroring on the customer gateway's ENI
VPC Flow Logs on the virtual private gateway's ENI
Site-to-Site VPN tunnel logs (IKE/IPsec events)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Site-to-Site VPN tunnel logs capture IKE and IPsec negotiation events that explain periodic drops.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail data events: not tunnel events.
• Traffic Mirroring on CGW: not available.
• Flow logs on VGW: not tunnel negotiation.

Key takeaway: diagnose VPN tunnel drops → tunnel logs.

stem: A company wants a single pair of Direct Connect connections at one colocation facility to provide private connectivity to VPCs in three different AWS Regions without provisioning separate physical connections in each Region. Which Direct Connect construct enables this?

choices.text: Three hosted VIFs, one per Region, on the same physical connection
A DX gateway associated with gateways in all three Regions
A single private VIF associated directly with a VGW in each Region
A transit VIF attached directly to VPCs in each Region

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Direct Connect gateway associated with gateways in all three Regions lets one pair of connections reach VPCs across Regions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hosted VIF per Region: unnecessary.
• Private VIF to VGWs in multiple Regions: a VIF attaches to one gateway.
• Transit VIF to VPCs directly: attaches to DX gateway.

Key takeaway: one DX, many Regions → DX gateway.

stem: A VPN attachment to a Transit Gateway shows both tunnels UP and the BGP session state as Established, but the on-premises routes are missing from the Transit Gateway route table associated with that attachment. What is the most likely misconfiguration?

choices.text: The Transit Gateway attachment is in the pending state and must be manually accepted
The VPN connection was created without a virtual private gateway, which is mandatory for Transit Gateway attachments
Route propagation has not been enabled from the VPN attachment into that specific Transit Gateway route table
The customer gateway ASN is a private ASN, which Transit Gateway does not support for VPN attachments

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With BGP established, routes still won't reach the TGW route table unless propagation from the VPN attachment is enabled (or static routes added).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Pending attachment: then tunnels wouldn't route at all.
• No VGW needed: TGW VPNs don't need one.
• Private ASN unsupported: supported.

Key takeaway: BGP up ≠ routes propagated.

stem: An organization wants Transit Gateway to load-balance (ECMP) traffic across two Site-to-Site VPN connections attached to the same Transit Gateway route table for higher aggregate throughput. Which two conditions must be true for this to work? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The VPN connections must be Accelerated VPNs using Global Accelerator
Both VPN connections must be attached in the same Availability Zone
Both VPN connections must share the same customer gateway IP address
Both connections must use BGP, not static routes
The propagated routes must be equal cost (prefix, AS path)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
TGW ECMP across VPN connections requires BGP dynamic routing and equal-cost routes (same prefixes and AS path length), with ECMP support enabled on the TGW.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Accelerated VPN required: no.
• Same AZ: not applicable.
• Same CGW IP: not required.

Key takeaway: VPN ECMP = BGP + equal routes.

stem: A Site-to-Site VPN tunnel to a branch office repeatedly drops during periods of low traffic, then re-establishes once traffic resumes. The on-premises device implements Dead Peer Detection (DPD) with aggressive timers, while AWS's side uses default DPD settings. What is the most likely cause and appropriate fix?

choices.text: The on-premises MTU is too large, so DPD packets are fragmented and dropped
Aggressive device DPD timers during idle periods; align them or keep traffic flowing
PFS is disabled, which AWS requires for idle tunnels to stay up
AWS endpoints don't support DPD, so it should be disabled on the customer gateway

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Aggressive DPD timers on the customer device during idle periods can tear down tunnels. Align DPD settings with AWS or keep traffic flowing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• MTU fragmenting DPD: unlikely.
• PFS required for idle tunnels: no.
• AWS doesn't support DPD: it does.

Key takeaway: idle drops → DPD settings.

stem: A company has a Direct Connect Link Aggregation Group (LAG) composed of four 10 Gbps connections and requires at least 20 Gbps of guaranteed aggregate bandwidth for compliance reasons. Which LAG setting should be configured so the LAG automatically goes down, forcing failover to a backup path, if fewer than two member connections remain active?

choices.text: Set the LAG's minimum_links parameter to 2
Set the LAG's MTU to 9001
Enable BFD on the LAG's virtual interfaces only
Reduce the number of physical connections in the LAG to 2

explanation:
Why this is correct:
minimum_links sets how many member connections must be up for the LAG to stay operational.

Why the other options are wrong:
• MTU: unrelated.
• BFD only: detection, not LAG threshold.
• Remove connections: reduces capacity.

Key takeaway: LAG availability threshold → minimum_links.

stem: A customer wants Direct Connect to prefer one of its two private virtual interfaces, both advertising the same on-premises routes, as the primary path for traffic from a VPC toward on-premises, using a mechanism AWS explicitly documents for signaling local preference rather than AS-path manipulation. What should the customer configure on the BGP sessions?

choices.text: Advertise a default route only on the preferred virtual interface
Configure a lower BGP hold timer on the preferred virtual interface
AWS local preference communities (high on preferred, low on backup)
Set a higher MED on the preferred virtual interface's routes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS local preference BGP communities (high on the preferred VIF, low on the backup) control which VIF AWS uses to reach on-premises.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Default route only: not the mechanism.
• Lower hold timer: detection only.
• Higher MED on preferred: makes it less preferred.

Key takeaway: steer AWS outbound → local preference communities.

stem: Before a change window, an engineer wants to prove, without sending traffic, whether an instance can reach an RDS endpoint in another VPC via TGW, and which component would block it. Which tool fits?

choices.text: Traffic Mirroring
CloudWatch Network Monitor probes between the endpoints
VPC Reachability Analyzer
VPC Flow Logs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Reachability Analyzer performs static analysis of configuration (routes, security groups, NACLs, TGW) between a source and destination, and names the blocking component, without sending packets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flow logs: show traffic that actually occurred.
• Traffic Mirroring: copies real packets.
• Network Monitor: measures real loss and latency with probes.

Key takeaway: 'would it work?' without traffic → Reachability Analyzer.

stem: An application team reports that instances in Subnet A cannot reach an internal Network Load Balancer's targets in Subnet B, despite security groups appearing correct. Using VPC Reachability Analyzer, the engineer analyzes the path from an instance ENI in Subnet A to a target ENI behind the NLB and receives a result of Not Reachable, with the blocking component identified as a network ACL rule in Subnet B. What should the engineer conclude and check?

choices.text: Reachability Analyzer evaluates only security groups
Reachability Analyzer can't analyze load balancer paths, so the result is invalid
Subnet B's NACL blocks the traffic; fix the rules it identified
It must be DNS, since Reachability Analyzer ignores Layer 3/4 constructs like NACLs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Reachability Analyzer identified Subnet B's NACL as the blocker. Fix those NACL rules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only SGs: it evaluates NACLs, routes, and more.
• Can't analyze load balancers: it can.
• DNS: it analyzes L3/L4 configuration.

Key takeaway: trust the component Reachability Analyzer names.

stem: A security team wants to send a copy of all traffic to and from a fleet of EC2 instances to a third-party intrusion detection appliance running behind a Gateway Load Balancer, for out-of-band deep packet inspection, without impacting the original traffic path or adding latency to production flows. Which VPC feature should be used?

choices.text: VPC peering between the application VPC and the IDS VPC
Flow logs with all traffic streamed to the IDS appliances through Firehose
VPC Traffic Mirroring to a target fronting the IDS fleet
AWS PrivateLink with an interface endpoint for the IDS appliances

explanation:
Why this is correct:
VPC Traffic Mirroring copies packets from ENIs to a target (such as an NLB or GWLB) fronting the IDS appliances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Peering: connectivity, not copies.
• Flow logs: metadata, not packets.
• PrivateLink: service access.

Key takeaway: packet copies for IDS → Traffic Mirroring.

stem: A team configures a Traffic Mirror session from a source ENI to a mirror target ENI in the same VPC, but the destination monitoring tool sees no packets. The mirror target's security group allows all inbound traffic from the VPC CIDR, and both the source and target are Nitro-based instances. What is a commonly overlooked requirement that should be checked next?

choices.text: The session's VXLAN network identifier must match the source subnet CIDR
Traffic Mirroring requires the source and target to be in the same subnet
Traffic Mirroring supports only internet-bound traffic, not intra-VPC traffic
The target must allow UDP 4789 (VXLAN) and the tool must decapsulate VXLAN

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Mirrored traffic arrives VXLAN-encapsulated on UDP 4789. The target's security group must allow it, and the tool must decapsulate it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VNI must match source: not the requirement.
• Same subnet required: no.
• Internet traffic only: no.

Key takeaway: mirror targets need UDP 4789 and VXLAN handling.

stem: A network operations team wants continuous, agent-based measurement of latency and packet loss along the specific paths between their on-premises data centers and their AWS VPCs over both Direct Connect and VPN, independent of whether the BGP session itself reports a failure, to catch brownout conditions like partial packet loss that do not take BGP down. Which AWS capability is designed for this?

choices.text: VPC Reachability Analyzer
Amazon CloudWatch Network Monitor
The AWS Direct Connect ConnectionBpsEgress CloudWatch metric alone
Amazon CloudWatch Internet Monitor

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudWatch Network Monitor uses probes to measure latency and packet loss continuously along hybrid paths.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reachability Analyzer: static configuration.
• DX egress metric: throughput only.
• Internet Monitor: internet paths to users.

Key takeaway: hybrid path quality → Network Monitor.

stem: A team troubleshooting NAT Gateway usage wants to see, for each flow, both the original (pre-NAT) source and destination addresses, in order to correlate specific EC2 instances with their outbound internet destinations at the NAT Gateway ENI. The default VPC Flow Logs format does not include this. Which two custom format fields should be added to the Flow Logs subscription to capture this information? (Select TWO)

choices.text: dstaddr
pkt-srcaddr
pkt-dstaddr
srcaddr
flow-direction

explanation:
Why this is correct:
pkt-srcaddr and pkt-dstaddr show the original packet addresses, revealing pre-NAT source and final destination alongside srcaddr and dstaddr.

Why the other options are wrong:
• dstaddr/srcaddr: interface-level addresses.
• flow-direction: direction only.

Key takeaway: see through NAT → pkt-* fields.

stem: Traffic Mirroring fails for a source ENI on an older instance type. What is the cause, and what fixes it?

choices.text: The source isn't Nitro-based; move to a Nitro instance type
Only one mirror session is allowed per VPC
The mirror target must be created first
The source ENI must be in a public subnet with an internet gateway route

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Traffic Mirroring requires sources on Nitro-based instance types. Changing the instance to a supported Nitro type resolves it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One session per VPC: not a restriction.
• Public subnet: not required.
• Target first: order isn't the issue.

Key takeaway: Traffic Mirroring = Nitro sources.

stem: A cloud security team wants to periodically scan an entire AWS Organization's VPCs to proactively find any unintended network paths that violate a defined security posture, for example any path allowing internet access to a database tier, rather than testing one specific source-destination pair at a time. Which tool is better suited to this broader, policy-based discovery compared to testing individual paths?

choices.text: AWS Config conformance packs alone, without network path analysis
Reachability Analyzer run manually for every pair of ENIs in the organization
Network Access Analyzer with defined access scopes
Amazon CloudWatch Network Monitor probes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Network Access Analyzer evaluates network paths against defined access scopes (for example, internet to sensitive subnets) across VPCs to find unintended access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Conformance packs: no path analysis.
• Reachability Analyzer per pair: not scalable.
• Network Monitor: performance probes.

Key takeaway: find unintended network paths → Network Access Analyzer.

stem: Application teams report intermittent packet loss for traffic sent over a single Site-to-Site VPN tunnel attached to a Transit Gateway, even though BGP is stable and the tunnel shows as UP. Utilization on the tunnel is consistently near 1.2 Gbps. Which conclusion and CloudWatch evidence best explains the drops?

choices.text: TGW has no per-tunnel limit, so the drops must come from an on-premises firewall
The ~1.25 Gbps per-tunnel limit; spread traffic with ECMP across tunnels
A NACL misconfiguration, shown by the PacketDropCountNoRoute metric
BGP route flapping, which would show as TunnelState oscillating between 0 and 1

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Each VPN tunnel supports about 1.25 Gbps. Exceeding it causes drops. Use ECMP across multiple tunnels or connections via TGW.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No per-tunnel limit: there is one.
• NACL: PacketDropCountNoRoute indicates routing.
• BGP flapping: would show state changes.

Key takeaway: VPN throughput → scale with ECMP.

stem: A company centralizes VPC Flow Logs from 50 AWS accounts into a single S3 bucket in a log-archive account, keyed by organization ID, account ID, region, and date. The security team wants to run ad hoc Athena queries filtered to a specific account and date range while keeping query costs low. What should they do when defining the Athena table?

choices.text: Use Redshift Spectrum, since Athena can't query data organized by nested prefixes
Copy each account's logs into a separate bucket, since Athena can't filter by account
One unpartitioned table over the bucket
Partition by account, Region, and date (projection or Glue)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Partitioning by account, Region, and date (with partition projection or Glue) lets Athena prune data and query efficiently.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Redshift Spectrum required: no.
• Separate buckets: unnecessary.
• Unpartitioned table: scans everything.

Key takeaway: large log sets → partitions.

stem: A Traffic Mirror filter has two rules: rule number 100 rejects all TCP traffic on port 22, and rule number 200 accepts all TCP traffic from the corporate CIDR block, which includes port 22. Engineers expected SSH traffic from the corporate CIDR to be mirrored but observe that it is not. What explains this behavior?

choices.text: Accept rules are always evaluated before reject rules, so this is a bug to report
Rule numbers don't affect order; matching rules combine with OR, so it should mirror
Lowest rule number first; the first match (reject 100) wins
Mirror filters can't filter by port, only protocol

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Mirror filter rules are evaluated from the lowest number. Rule 100 (reject TCP 22) matches first.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Accept before reject: no.
• OR combination: no.
• Can't filter ports: they can.

Key takeaway: lowest rule number first.

stem: A hybrid network team notices application-level timeouts between an on-premises data center and a VPC during business hours, but Direct Connect's BGP session remains Established and the DX ConnectionState metric shows Up throughout. They suspect intermittent partial packet loss on the underlying circuit that is not severe enough to bring down BGP. Which approach provides the most direct, quantitative confirmation of this brownout condition on the specific path?

choices.text: Rely on ConnectionState and ConnectionBpsEgress
Raise the BGP hold timer so minor packet loss is tolerated and not flagged
Network Monitor probes measuring loss and latency on the path
Open a case and wait for a Health Dashboard event, since brownouts can't be detected

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Network Monitor probes measure packet loss and latency on the path, revealing gray failures that connection state metrics miss.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ConnectionState only: misses brownouts.
• Longer hold timer: hides issues.
• Wait for Health events: slow.

Key takeaway: brownouts → active probing.

stem: A startup needs encrypted connectivity from its office to a VPC this week, with about 200 Mbps of unpredictable traffic, while it evaluates Direct Connect over the next quarter. Which option fits, and what is its main limitation?

choices.text: Site-to-Site VPN; each tunnel tops out around 1.25 Gbps
VPC peering to the office network over the internet
A dedicated 10 Gbps Direct Connect port, which is always cheaper than VPN
A hosted Direct Connect connection, which encrypts traffic by default

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Site-to-Site VPN is IPsec-encrypted, can be set up in minutes with no long-term commitment, and easily carries 200 Mbps. Its main limit is per-tunnel throughput (about 1.25 Gbps) over the variable internet path.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Dedicated 10 Gbps DX: takes weeks to provision, and port hours are costly for 200 Mbps.
• Hosted DX: not encrypted by default, and provisioning takes time through a partner.
• VPC peering: connects VPCs only, not on-premises networks.

Key takeaway: fast, encrypted, low commitment → VPN; consistent high bandwidth → Direct Connect.

stem: A company runs many EC2 instances in private subnets that make frequent calls to Amazon S3 and DynamoDB, currently routed through a NAT Gateway. The monthly bill shows a significant NAT Gateway data processing charge. What is the most effective way to reduce this specific cost while keeping the traffic off the public internet?

choices.text: Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance
Add multiple Elastic IP addresses to the NAT gateway to spread the load
Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB to bypass the NAT
Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) for S3 and DynamoDB, cheaper than NAT

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB route that traffic privately, bypassing NAT processing charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NAT instance: still in the path.
• More EIPs: no cost reduction.
• Interface endpoints cheaper than gateway: gateway endpoints are free.

Key takeaway: S3/DynamoDB → gateway endpoints.

stem: An application uses AWS Global Accelerator with two Application Load Balancer endpoints in different Regions within the same endpoint group, configured with equal endpoint weights, both currently healthy. Operations wants to gradually shift a small percentage of new connections to the newly added Region without a hard cutover, in order to validate performance before increasing its share. Which Global Accelerator setting should be adjusted?

choices.text: Lower the new Region endpoint's weight relative to the existing Region's endpoint
Change the health check protocol from HTTP to TCP to slow traffic shifting
Set the new endpoint group's traffic dial to 100% with equal endpoint weights
Switch client affinity from None to Source IP for a gradual rollout

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Endpoint weights control the share of traffic within an endpoint group. Setting a lower weight on the new endpoint sends it less traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• TCP health checks: not traffic control.
• Traffic dial 100% equal weights: no gradual shift.
• Source IP affinity: stickiness.

Key takeaway: within-group shares → endpoint weights.

stem: After migrating a batch-processing workload to instances that support jumbo frames (9001 MTU) within a VPC, throughput improved for traffic between instances in the same VPC. However, traffic from these instances to an on-premises data center over a Site-to-Site VPN now experiences intermittent stalls and retransmissions for larger payloads. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: It's unrelated to MTU and caused by the VPN's fixed per-tunnel bandwidth cap
VPN requires jumbo frames end to end, so raise the on-prem router MTU to 9001
Jumbo frames work only within one subnet, so VPC-level jumbo traffic drops randomly
IPsec overhead lowers the path MTU; oversized packets drop without MSS clamping

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IPsec overhead reduces the path MTU below 9001. Without working PMTUD or MSS clamping, oversized packets are dropped.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Per-tunnel throughput: different symptom.
• Raise on-prem to jumbo: VPN doesn't support it.
• Jumbo within one subnet only: false.

Key takeaway: VPN lowers path MTU.

stem: A three-tier application has web, application, and database tiers spread evenly across three Availability Zones for high availability. The monthly bill shows substantial inter-AZ data transfer charges from chatty communication between the application and database tiers. Without reducing the number of AZs used for availability, what is a reasonable strategy to reduce inter-AZ data transfer costs for this traffic pattern?

choices.text: Enable VPC Flow Logs, which compress records and reduce cross-AZ traffic
AZ-aware routing to same-AZ replicas or cache nodes
Move all tiers into one AZ to eliminate inter-AZ charges entirely
Replace the VPC with a Transit Gateway, whose traffic is free within a Region

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-AZ data transfer is charged. Routing requests to same-AZ replicas or cache nodes reduces cross-AZ traffic while keeping multi-AZ resilience.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flow Logs compress traffic: no.
• Single AZ: loses resilience.
• TGW free: no.

Key takeaway: AZ-aware routing reduces transfer costs.

stem: A mid-size company needs approximately 2 Gbps of dedicated private connectivity to AWS and wants to minimize both cost and the complexity of managing physical cross-connects, and is willing to depend on a Direct Connect Partner for the local loop and port. Which connection type best matches this requirement compared to provisioning a dedicated connection?

choices.text: A dedicated 10 Gbps connection, which is always cheaper per Gbps than hosted
A ~2 Gbps partner hosted connection (no LAG)
A hosted VIF, which provides the physical cross-connect unlike hosted connections
Two 1 Gbps dedicated connections in a LAG

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A partner hosted connection at about 2 Gbps matches the needed capacity without paying for 10 Gbps or managing a LAG.

Why the other options are wrong:
• 10 Gbps always cheaper: overprovisioned.
• Hosted VIF provides cross-connect: incorrect.
• Two 1 Gbps in a LAG: more cost and complexity.

Key takeaway: right-size DX capacity.

stem: A gaming company runs a UDP-based multiplayer backend in two AWS Regions and needs clients worldwide to connect to the nearest healthy backend with automatic failover, using a small set of static anycast IP addresses that must never change because they are allowlisted in restrictive corporate and school firewalls. Which service best fits this requirement, and why is the likely alternative less suitable?

choices.text: Neither supports UDP, so a custom ELB-based solution is required
Global Accelerator, only because it's cheaper; both support UDP and static IPs
Global Accelerator (static anycast IPs, TCP/UDP, health-based routing)
CloudFront, whose edges give the lowest latency for any protocol including UDP

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Global Accelerator supports TCP and UDP with static anycast IPs and health-based Regional failover.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Neither supports UDP: Global Accelerator does.
• Only cheaper: capability is the reason.
• CloudFront any protocol: HTTP(S) only.

Key takeaway: UDP multi-Region → Global Accelerator.

stem: Large HTTPS downloads from an on-premises client to a server in AWS over a Site-to-Site VPN hang indefinitely after the initial TLS handshake completes, while small requests work fine. The on-premises firewall blocks all inbound ICMP as a security policy. What is the most likely root cause and fix?

choices.text: A DNS issue, since only large downloads trigger a fresh DNS lookup
The IKE phase 2 lifetime is too short, causing rekeys that affect large transfers
PMTUD black hole from blocked ICMP; allow it or clamp MSS
The tunnel's maximum concurrent connection count has been exceeded

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Large transfers hang when ICMP 'fragmentation needed' messages are blocked, breaking PMTUD. Allow ICMP or clamp TCP MSS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DNS: unrelated.
• IKE lifetime: different symptom.
• Connection limits: not the cause.

Key takeaway: large transfers hang over VPN → PMTUD black hole.

stem: A large enterprise with 30 AWS accounts under AWS Organizations currently has separate Direct Connect connections purchased for several business units, resulting in high fixed port-hour costs and complex cross-connect management. They want to consolidate to a smaller number of physical connections while still giving each business unit's VPCs private connectivity to on-premises. What is a cost-effective architectural approach?

choices.text: A few DX connections shared via a DX gateway and TGW for all accounts
One DX connection per account, since connections can't be shared across accounts
Share EC2 instances across accounts with RAM to avoid more DX connections
Per-account Site-to-Site VPNs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A few DX connections shared via a Direct Connect gateway and Transit Gateway serve all accounts, reducing cost and complexity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Connection per account: expensive.
• Share EC2 via RAM: nonsensical.
• VPNs per account: not dedicated connectivity.

Key takeaway: share DX across accounts via DX gateway + TGW.

stem: During a Regional deployment rollout, operations wants Global Accelerator to send a controlled 10 percent of an accelerator's traffic to a newly deployed endpoint group in a second Region while the remaining 90 percent continues to the original Region, in order to validate the new deployment under partial production load before a full cutover. Which setting should they configure, and at what scope does it apply?

choices.text: Set each endpoint's weight in the new group to 10, limiting that Region to 10%
Set the health check interval to 10 seconds to achieve a 10% split
Set the new Region endpoint group's traffic dial to 10%
Enable Source IP client affinity with a 10% sampling rate

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The traffic dial on an endpoint group controls the percentage of traffic directed to that Region's group.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Weights: share within a group.
• Health check interval: no.
• Source IP sampling: doesn't exist.

Key takeaway: Regional traffic share → traffic dial.

stem: After migrating a workload to a current-generation EC2 instance type rated for up to 25 Gbps of network bandwidth, an application team observes actual throughput capped at roughly 5 Gbps between two instances in the same VPC and placement group. CPU utilization on both instances is low. What should be checked first?

choices.text: Whether the VPC's DHCP option set lists the correct domain name servers
Whether a NAT gateway is in the path
Whether the ENA driver is installed and current
Whether the security group has a rule explicitly limiting bandwidth

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Enhanced networking needs the ENA driver installed and current. Without it, instances don't reach their rated bandwidth.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DHCP options: DNS.
• NAT gateway: not the limit here.
• SG bandwidth limits: don't exist.

Key takeaway: high network throughput → ENA driver.

stem: A media company transfers large volumes of data, over 500 TB per month, from AWS to an on-premises data center. They are deciding between continuing to send this traffic over the public internet using standard internet data transfer out pricing, versus provisioning a Direct Connect connection and sending it over a private virtual interface. Which statement correctly describes the typical cost tradeoff involved?

choices.text: Internet egress becomes free above 500 TB per month, removing any DX advantage
DX egress has a lower per-GB rate, likely offsetting port-hour fees
DX egress costs the same per GB as internet egress
Data transfer over Direct Connect is free at any volume once provisioned

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data transfer out over Direct Connect has a lower per-GB rate than internet egress. At 500 TB per month, savings likely outweigh port-hour costs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Free internet egress: false.
• Same rate: DX is lower.
• Free DX transfer: false.

Key takeaway: high egress volumes favor DX.

stem: A security engineer configures an AWS Network Firewall policy with a stateless default action of aws:forward_to_sfe, plus a stateless rule group containing one rule that matches TCP traffic on destination port 443 with the action aws:pass. After deployment, outbound HTTPS connections from the protected subnet initiate successfully, but responses from the internet never arrive and the connections eventually time out. What is the most likely cause and correct fix?

choices.text: Stateless rule groups cannot match TCP 443; only stateful groups match ports.
aws:pass skips state tracking, so return traffic misses; forward to a stateful PASS rule.
The firewall subnet's route table lacks a route back to the internet gateway, black-holing replies.
Network Firewall needs a NAT gateway in the firewall subnet for TLS handshakes to complete.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A stateless pass action forwards packets without state tracking, so return traffic isn't recognized as part of the flow. Forward traffic to the stateful engine (aws:forward_to_sfe) so return traffic is handled.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stateless can't match 443: it can.
• Missing route: not indicated.
• NAT for TLS: not required.

Key takeaway: use stateful inspection for bidirectional flows.

stem: A company manages an AWS Network Firewall policy with multiple stateful rule groups: one using domain list rules to allow specific FQDNs and another using 5-tuple rules to deny known malicious CIDR ranges. Auditors require that the firewall evaluate rule groups in a specific, predictable sequence and that any traffic not explicitly matched be dropped, regardless of the order in which rule groups were attached to the policy. Which configuration should the engineer implement?

choices.text: Put all rules in one stateless rule group.
Strict order, explicit group priorities, and a strict default drop.
Use Suricata rules with the alert action only, since alerts need no explicit order.
Use default action order and rely on the implicit pass-if-no-match behavior.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Strict rule order with explicit rule group priorities and a strict default action (such as drop established) makes evaluation predictable across groups.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One stateless group: loses stateful features.
• Alert only: doesn't enforce.
• Default action order: less predictable.

Key takeaway: predictable firewall policies → strict order.

stem: A network security team wants AWS Network Firewall to detect and block outbound traffic containing a specific known malware command-and-control byte pattern within the TCP payload, in addition to existing IP- and port-based filtering. Which stateful rule format should they use to add this capability?

choices.text: Domain list rules referencing only the malware's known C2 domain names.
Suricata-compatible IPS rule strings that match specific content within the packet payload.
Standard stateful 5-tuple rules, since Network Firewall automatically performs deep packet inspection on every 5-tuple match.
Stateless 5-tuple rules matching the destination port historically associated with the malware.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Suricata-compatible IPS rules can match specific payload content and signatures, blocking malware traffic even when domains change.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Domain lists: miss unknown or changing domains.
• 5-tuple rules detecting malware automatically: no.
• Stateless port rules: too coarse.

Key takeaway: content inspection → Suricata IPS rules.

stem: An engineer created a stateful Suricata-compatible rule group in AWS Network Firewall with a capacity of 100 and later needs to add enough additional rules that the required capacity would exceed 100. What must the engineer do?

choices.text: Attach a second rule group with the same name; Network Firewall merges same-name groups.
Ask AWS Support to raise the account quota.
Create a larger new group, migrate rules, and update the policy.
Edit the rule group and increase its capacity value directly at any time.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Rule group capacity is fixed at creation. Create a larger group, migrate the rules, and update the policy to use it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Duplicate names: not allowed.
• Support quota: capacity isn't a quota.
• Edit capacity: can't change.

Key takeaway: capacity is immutable → recreate larger.

stem: A rate-based rule in an AWS WAF web ACL uses an aggregate key type of IP with a limit of 2,000 requests per 5-minute window, evaluating the client IP as seen by WAF. The application sits behind Amazon CloudFront and a security appliance, so all viewer requests arrive at WAF from the appliance's single IP address. The rule now blocks all legitimate users during peak traffic, while a slow, distributed attack from thousands of unique IPs goes undetected. What should the engineer do?

choices.text: Move rate limiting to Shield Advanced.
Raise the rate limit so peak traffic isn't blocked, leaving the attack unmitigated.
Aggregate on a trusted forwarded-IP header.
Aggregate all requests under a single constant key with one global counter.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If traffic arrives through a proxy or CDN, aggregating on IP counts the proxy's IP. Aggregate on a trusted forwarded-IP header to rate-limit real clients.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shield Advanced: not rate limiting per client.
• Raise the limit: doesn't fix aggregation.
• Single global key: blocks everyone together.

Key takeaway: rate-limit the real client IP.

stem: A central security team must ensure that every Application Load Balancer created in any of 40 accounts within an AWS Organizations organization automatically has a standard AWS WAF web ACL, containing baseline managed rule groups, attached, and that individual account owners cannot detach or override it. Which approach meets this requirement with the least ongoing operational effort?

choices.text: A Firewall Manager WAF policy enforced across the org.
Create the web ACL in each account and use an SCP to deny WAF disassociation.
Share the web ACL through RAM and have teams associate it with their ALBs manually.
A Config rule with SSM auto-remediation that reattaches the web ACL when missing.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Firewall Manager WAF policy applies the web ACL to every ALB across the organization, including new ones.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Per-account ACLs with SCP: toil.
• RAM-shared web ACL: teams must associate manually.
• Config remediation: reactive.

Key takeaway: org-wide WAF → Firewall Manager.

stem: A customer asks how WAF and Shield Advanced differ for an API under both SQL injection attempts and volumetric DDoS. Which answer is correct?

choices.text: WAF filters L7 requests; Shield Advanced adds DDoS defense and support
Shield Advanced replaces WAF by blocking malicious payloads without rules
Both work only at Layer 3/4
WAF must be bought with Shield Advanced

explanation:
Why this is correct:
WAF inspects HTTP requests (SQL injection, rate limits). Shield Advanced adds enhanced DDoS detection and mitigation (including L7 with a web ACL), the Shield Response Team, and cost protection.

Why the other options are wrong:
• L3/4 only: WAF is L7.
• Bundled purchase: WAF is standalone (Shield Advanced includes WAF usage for protected resources, but WAF doesn't require it).
• Replaces WAF: Shield uses WAF for L7 mitigation.

Key takeaway: WAF = request filtering; Shield Advanced = DDoS resilience + support.

stem: A company has Shield Advanced on an internet-facing ALB and wants automatic application-layer DDoS mitigation, with rules created and removed during attacks without manual work. What is required?

choices.text: Put the ALB behind CloudFront, since automatic L7 mitigation works only there
Associate a WAF web ACL with the ALB and enable automatic mitigation
Use a fixed target group without Auto Scaling
Disable AWS WAF, since Shield Advanced replaces its rule engine

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced's automatic application layer mitigation places rules in a WAF web ACL associated with the protected resource. Without a web ACL on the ALB, it has nowhere to put mitigation rules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudFront only: ALBs are supported when a web ACL is associated.
• Disabling WAF: removes the mechanism mitigation depends on.
• Fixed target group: unrelated to mitigation.

Key takeaway: Shield Advanced L7 auto-mitigation = rules inside your WAF web ACL.

stem: During an active, severe DDoS attack against a Shield Advanced protected AWS Global Accelerator resource, a customer wants to engage the AWS Shield Response Team (SRT) for emergency assistance crafting custom mitigations. What must be true for the customer to engage the SRT?

choices.text: SRT engagement is available only for resources also protected by Network Firewall.
The customer must first open a case with the Trust & Safety team before the SRT engages.
Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, or Enterprise Support is required.
Any Basic Support customer can reach the SRT.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Engaging the Shield Response Team requires Shield Advanced plus Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, or Enterprise Support.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only with CloudFront: no.
• Trust & Safety case: no.
• Basic Support: not eligible.

Key takeaway: SRT needs a qualifying Support plan.

stem: A customer has an active Shield Advanced subscription at the account level. During a volumetric UDP reflection attack targeting an EC2 instance's Elastic IP address used for a custom UDP application, the customer expects enhanced Shield Advanced detection and mitigation metrics in the console but sees none for that resource. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: Elastic IPs aren't eligible for Shield Advanced and get only Standard defenses.
Shield Advanced never inspects UDP traffic, only TCP-based attacks.
A subscription protects everything automatically.
The Elastic IP was never added as a protected resource.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced protects only resources explicitly added as protected resources. The Elastic IP wasn't added.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EIPs ineligible: they're eligible.
• No UDP inspection: UDP attacks are covered.
• Automatic coverage: must add resources.

Key takeaway: add each resource to Shield Advanced.

stem: Instances in a private subnet can successfully initiate outbound HTTPS connections to an external API, and security group rules correctly allow the outbound request and its stateful return traffic. Connections still fail, however. The subnet's network ACL has an inbound rule allowing TCP port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 and an outbound rule allowing TCP port 443 to 0.0.0.0/0, with all other traffic implicitly denied. What is the cause?

choices.text: NACLs support only outbound rules, so inbound rules are ignored for private subnets.
Security groups are stateless and need an explicit inbound rule for responses.
NACL rules are evaluated in reverse order.
NACLs are stateless; allow inbound ephemeral ports for the replies.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
NACLs are stateless, so responses to outbound requests need inbound rules for ephemeral ports.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Outbound only: NACLs have both.
• SGs stateless: they're stateful.
• Reverse order: lowest number first.

Key takeaway: stateless NACLs need return-port rules.

stem: An app tier accepts traffic only from a web tier. Both scale dynamically across 3 AZs, and IPs change constantly. Which rule fits?

choices.text: Reference the web SG ID in the app subnet's NACL
App SG inbound: allow the web tier's security group
Add each web instance IP as a /32 rule
Allow the whole VPC CIDR in the app tier SG

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security group references allow traffic from any ENI in the referenced group, regardless of IP, so scaling needs no rule changes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Whole VPC CIDR: too broad.
• NACL SG reference: NACLs can't reference security groups.
• /32 per instance: breaks with scaling and hits rule limits.

Key takeaway: reference security groups, not IPs.

stem: A network engineer adds a new NACL rule with rule number 50 that denies inbound traffic from a specific malicious CIDR block. Shortly after, legitimate traffic from an unrelated, previously allowed CIDR range starts being blocked as well. The existing allow rule for that legitimate range has rule number 100. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: Lowest number first; rule 50 matched the legitimate range too.
Rule 50 applies only to outbound traffic.
Adding any deny rule inverts the default action for every other rule in the ACL.
NACLs evaluate all matching rules and apply the most restrictive one.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
NACL rules are evaluated lowest number first and the first match applies. Rule 50's range also covered legitimate traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Outbound only: it's inbound.
• Inverts defaults: no.
• Most restrictive: first match wins.

Key takeaway: check NACL deny ranges and order.

stem: A security team needs to allow inbound access from over 200 corporate office CIDR ranges to a fleet of application servers, but the default security group rule quota per security group makes maintaining individual CIDR rules impractical, and they also want to update every associated security group in one place when office ranges change. What should they implement?

choices.text: A customer-managed prefix list referenced in one rule.
Request an unlimited rule quota and keep adding each CIDR as its own rule.
Use a NACL instead, since NACLs allow unlimited CIDR rules with no quota.
Create 200 security groups, one per CIDR, and attach them all to every instance.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A customer-managed prefix list holds all 200 CIDRs and is referenced in one security group rule, staying within quotas and easy to update.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Unlimited rules: quotas exist.
• NACLs unlimited: also limited and stateless.
• 200 SGs: impractical.

Key takeaway: many CIDRs → prefix lists.

stem: A security team enables VPC Flow Logs to capture all rejected traffic for a subnet containing EC2 instances that resolve internal hostnames using the VPC's Amazon-provided DNS resolver. During an audit, they cannot find any flow log records showing DNS queries from the instances to that resolver, even though other traffic is logged correctly. What is the reason?

choices.text: Flow logs exclude Amazon DNS traffic; use Resolver query logging.
The 10-minute aggregation interval is too long to capture short DNS flows.
DNS uses UDP, and flow logs capture only TCP traffic by default.
DNS is excluded unless the custom format includes a dns-query field.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Flow logs don't capture traffic to the Amazon DNS resolver. Use Resolver query logging for DNS visibility.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Interval too long: not the reason.
• UDP excluded: flow logs include UDP.
• dns-query field: doesn't exist.

Key takeaway: DNS visibility → Resolver query logs.

stem: Traffic from EC2 instances in a private subnet passes through a NAT gateway before reaching the internet. Default-format VPC Flow Logs for the NAT gateway's ENI show the NAT gateway's own IP address as both srcaddr and dstaddr for translated flows, making it impossible to identify which private instance originated a suspicious outbound connection. How should the team reconfigure flow logs to solve this?

choices.text: Enable flow logs on each instance's ENI, since instance-level logs ignore NAT.
A custom format with pkt-srcaddr and pkt-dstaddr.
Set a 1-minute aggregation interval so pre-NAT addresses are captured.
Send flow logs to CloudWatch Logs.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A custom flow log format with pkt-srcaddr and pkt-dstaddr shows the original instance addresses behind the NAT gateway.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Instance ENI logs only: doesn't show post-NAT.
• 1-minute interval: unrelated.
• CloudWatch destination: unrelated.

Key takeaway: NAT visibility → pkt-* fields.

stem: A security team stores VPC Flow Logs in Amazon S3 in Parquet format and wants to identify potential port-scanning activity, characterized by a single source IP address generating many REJECT-action records against numerous distinct destination ports on the same destination IP within a short time window. Which approach detects this pattern at scale without building custom log-processing infrastructure?

choices.text: Have GuardDuty disable delivery, since Athena can't query Parquet flow logs.
Download and search each file manually for REJECT and count matches per file.
Athena SQL on REJECTs, counting distinct ports per source in a window.
Enable WAF logging on the VPC.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Athena can query Parquet flow logs with SQL, counting distinct destination ports per source among REJECTs in a time window to find scans.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Athena can't query Parquet: it can.
• Manual file search: impractical.
• WAF logging: HTTP only.

Key takeaway: detect port scans with Athena.

stem: An auditor asks whether AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress and CreateVpc calls are captured by a trail with default settings, and for how long they're queryable without a trail. Which answer is correct?

choices.text: Neither is logged unless data events are enabled
Only CreateVpc is logged by default; security group changes need data events
Both are management events; event history keeps 90 days
VPC API calls appear only in VPC Flow Logs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Both calls change resource configuration, so they are management events logged by default. CloudTrail event history shows 90 days of management events even without a trail; a trail stores them long-term.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Data events: those are object- or item-level operations.
• Only CreateVpc: both are management events.
• Flow logs: capture traffic, not API calls.

Key takeaway: configuration changes = management events.

stem: A central security account expects to see CloudTrail records for a VPC peering connection acceptance (ec2:AcceptVpcPeeringConnection) performed in a member account's ap-southeast-2 region, but the organization trail configured in the management account shows no such event. The organization trail was created as a single-region trail in us-east-1. What is the issue?

choices.text: The trail is single-Region; make it multi-Region (and organization-wide).
Organization trails can't capture EC2 networking events, only IAM events.
The member account must enable its own trail, since org trails skip networking calls.
Peering acceptance is logged only in the requester's Region, here us-east-1.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A single-Region trail misses events from other Regions. Make it multi-Region (and organization-wide).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Org trails can't capture EC2 networking: they can.
• Member must have own trail: org trails cover members.
• Requester's Region only: acceptance is logged where it happens.

Key takeaway: multi-Region trails capture all Regions.

stem: A company wants to automatically revoke any inbound security group rule that opens port 3389 (RDP) to 0.0.0.0/0 within seconds of it being created, using near real-time detection of the API call rather than periodic compliance scans. Which architecture best achieves this?

choices.text: Enable GuardDuty, wait for an UnauthorizedAccess finding.
A Config rule on a 24-hour periodic trigger with SSM Automation remediation.
Use VPC Flow Logs to detect RDP traffic and remediate after a connection is seen.
EventBridge on AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress invoking a revoking Lambda.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
